title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
會試録序
維
聖天子登極紀元之初載天下之
士舊貢新薦各随其道里近
逺以其有司續食勸駕之故
先後漸至自□嗣歲之春羣
有□□□者矣會試之期
===
既□□□書臣夔度閱籍
數之得三千一百有餘人嘆
曰烏戲盛矣非
皇上懋昭大徳纘承
祖宗作成樂育其曷能俾日月照
臨之域穷髮含齒之屬莫不
□俊乂以來其盛臻茲也
alt_text:
會試錄序
維
聖天子登極紀元之初載天下之
士舊貢新薦各隨其道里近
遠以其有司續食勸駕之致
先後漸至自二月歲之春暮
有□者矣會試之期
===
既□書臣□□□□
數之得三千一百有餘人嘆
曰爲盛矣非
皇上懋昭大德纘承
祖宗作成樂育甚昜餘俾日月照
臨之域窮髮含齒之區莫不
□俊又以來其盛□□□
punctuated:
會試録序

維聖天子登極紀元之初載，天下之士，舊貢新薦，各随其道里近逺，以其有司續食勸駕之故，先後漸至。自□嗣歲之春，羣有□□□者矣。會試之期既□，□□書臣夔度閱籍數之，得三千一百有餘人。嘆曰：「烏戲，盛矣！非皇上懋昭大徳，纘承祖宗作成樂育，其曷能俾日月照臨之域、穷髮含齒之屬，莫不□俊乂以來，其盛臻茲也？」
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the first year of the reign era following the Sacred Son of Heaven's ascension to the throne, the scholars of the realm—both formerly presented and newly recommended—gradually arrived one after another in accordance with the distance of their journeys, having been provided with travel rations and urged to set forth by their local authorities. From [?] the spring of the succeeding year, they had gathered [?]. When the date of the Metropolitan Examination arrived [?], your servant [Yao] Kui (姚夔), Minister [of Rites] [?], examined the registers and counted them, finding more than three thousand one hundred men. Reviewing this, I sighed and said: "Ah, how flourishing this is! Were it not that His Majesty exertively manifests his great virtue and continues the work of the Imperial Ancestors in cultivating and joyfully nurturing talent, how could it be brought about that throughout the realms illuminated by the sun and moon, among all hair-bearing and tooth-possessing humankind, none fail to [send forth?] men of outstanding ability to come here, reaching such a pinnacle of flourishing as this?" …

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
入對
黼坐以考官爲請有
詔以命學士臣定之臣安其同考
則侍讀臣吉修撰臣一夔臣讓
編修臣直臣永通臣環臣諧臣
元禎臣鉞給事中臣裕郎中臣宜
監試則御史臣綱
□掌悉從所推擇
臣定之辭不獲惴慄拜
命往暨其儕誓之而後將事乃
辛巳之日初試以孔曾思孟
之爲書易詩書春秋禮記之
爲經微辭奧旨發揚以類蓋
根本之學也越三日甲申再
alt_text:
入對
黼坐以考官爲請有
詔以命學士〔臣定之臣安〕其同考
則侍讀〔臣吉〕修撰〔臣一夔臣讓〕
編修〔臣直臣永通臣環臣誥臣元禎臣鉞〕僉十〔臣裕〕郎中〔臣宜〕
試則御史〔臣綱〕
===
掌憲從所推擇
〔臣定之〕辭不獲惴慄拜
命往暨其儕誓之而後將事乃
辛巳之日初試以孔曾思孟
之言書易詩書春秋禮記之
爲經微辭奥旨發揚以類蓋
根本之學也越二日甲申再
punctuated: 入對黼坐，以考官爲請。有詔以命學士臣定之、臣安；其同考則侍讀臣吉，修撰臣一夔、臣讓，編修臣直、臣永通、臣環、臣諧、臣元禎、臣鉞，給事中臣裕，郎中臣宜；監試則御史臣綱。□掌悉從所推擇。臣定之辭不獲，惴慄拜命，往暨其儕誓之，而後將事。乃辛巳之日，初試以孔、曾、思、孟之爲書，《易》、《詩》、《書》、《春秋》、《禮記》之爲經，微辭奧旨，發揚以類，蓋根本之學也。越三日甲申，再
translation_en: …entered into audience before the imperial throne to request the appointment of Examiners. An imperial edict was issued appointing Chancellors Your Servant [Liu] Dingzhi 劉定之 and Your Servant [Wan] An 萬安; for Associate Examiners, Academician Reader-in-Waiting Your Servant [Peng] Ji 彭吉, Senior Compilers Your Servant [Lu] Yikui 陸一夔 and Your Servant [Zheng] Rang 鄭讓, Junior Compilers Your Servant [Yin] Zhi 尹直, Your Servant [Chen] Yongtong 陳永通, Your Servant [Zhang] Huan 張環, Your Servant [Wu] Xie 吳諧, Your Servant [Zhang] Yuanzhen 張元禎, and Your Servant [Wang] Yue 王鉞, Supervising Secretary Your Servant Yu 裕, and Bureau Director Your Servant Yi 宜; and for Surveillance Commissioner of the Examination, Censor Your Servant Gang 綱. The remaining [?] posts were all filled in accordance with those nominated and selected. Your Servant Dingzhi sought to decline the appointment without success; trembling with awe, I bowed to receive the Imperial Mandate, proceeded there, took an oath together with my colleagues, and only then undertook the duties. On the xinsi day [the 9th day of the 2nd lunar month], the first session was held, examining them on the Four Books of Confucius, Zengzi, Zisi, and Mencius, and the Five Classics—the Book of Changes (Yi), Book of Odes (Shi), Book of Documents (Shu), Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), and Record of Rites (Liji)—whose subtle words and profound meanings were expounded according to their categories; this indeed represents fundamental learning. Three days later, on the jiashen day [the 12th], they were again…

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
試以論義理敷君上德意陳
臣下懇誠判决政刑散言儷
語唯所當則葩藻之藝也又
越三日丁亥終試之以古今
策牘山蘊海藏百為庶務其
施於用者奚宜斯又枝榦之
材然也若是者雖循往轍而
===
條畫加嚴如鎖院早一日嚴
故也揭曉亦早一日嚴所致
也試之初陰曀豁于晝月星
朗于夕既而自弦徂望霽景
益融天意開恱可知焉豈非
聖德所感也哉得士之尤者三百
五十人遵
alt_text:

臣下悃誠判決政刑散言儷
語唯所當則範藻之藝也又
越三日丁亥終試之以古今
策牘山蘊海藏百爲庶務其
施於用者〔多〕〔室〕斯又枝餘之
材然也若是者雖循往轍而
===
條畫加嚴如鎖院早一日嚴
故也揭曉亦早一日嚴所致
也試之初陰曀谿于晝月星
朗于夕既而自弦徂望霽景
益融天意開悅可知焉豈非
聖德所感也哉得士之尤者三百
五十人遵
punctuated: 試以論義理、敷君上德意、陳臣下懇誠、判决政刑，散言儷語，唯所當則，葩藻之藝也。又越三日丁亥，終試之以古今策牘，山蘊海藏，百為庶務，其施於用者奚宜，斯又枝榦之材然也。若是者雖循往轍，而條畫加嚴。如鎖院早一日，嚴故也；揭曉亦早一日，嚴所致也。試之初，陰曀豁于晝，月星朗于夕，既而自弦徂望，霽景益融，天意開恱可知焉，豈非聖德所感也哉！得士之尤者三百五十人，遵
translation_en: …examined them in discoursing on moral principles, proclaiming the sovereign's benevolent intentions, setting forth the earnest sincerity of subjects, and adjudicating administrative and penal matters—whether in prose or parallel style, each according to its proper standard—for these are the arts of literary floridity. After another three days, on the dinghai day, we finally examined them with policy questions on ancient and modern affairs—knowledge stored like mountains and seas, the myriad undertakings and general affairs, and how they may be suitably applied in practice—for such is the timber of branches and trunks. Although these procedures followed past precedent, the regulations and arrangements were made even stricter. For instance, the examination compound was locked a day earlier because of this strictness; the announcement of results also took place a day earlier, which was likewise an outcome of this strictness. At the beginning of the examination, overcast skies cleared during the day, and the moon and stars shone brightly at night. Thereafter, from the quarter moon to the full moon, the clear weather grew ever milder. That Heaven's will was pleased can thus be known—how could this not be a response to the sage virtue of Your Majesty! We obtained three hundred and fifty of the finest scholars, in compliance with…

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
聖斷也其視前科加多矣勒氏名
及文仰塵乙夜之
覽俯以示式于承學臣定之拜稽
言曰
皇朝得士以隆熈皞之運今百餘
年而皆以儒術造就之不用
他道盖與二帝三之時同彼
===
漢文景猶未能罷黜百家表
章六經唐終其祚常以詩賦
取材宋仁宗以後乃用經義
而濂洛所明者尚見擯棄也
豈若今用儒之純哉用之純
者得效必大且久以臣觀之
每科必有傑然偉人如亘天
alt_text:
聖斷也其視前科加多矣勒氏名
及文仰塵乙夜之
覽俯以示式于承學〔臣定之〕拜稽
言曰
皇朝得士以隆熙皡之運今百餘
年而皆以儒術造就之不用
他道蓋與二帝三王之時同彼
===
漢文景猶未能罷黜百家表
章六經唐終其祚常以詩賦
取材宋仁宗以後乃用經義
而濂洛所明者尚見擯棄也
豈若今用儒之純哉用之純
者得效必大且久以〔臣〕觀之
每科必有傑然偉人如亘天
punctuated: 聖斷也，其視前科加多矣。勒氏名及文，仰塵乙夜之覽，俯以示式于承學。臣定之拜稽言曰：皇朝得士以隆熈皞之運，今百餘年，而皆以儒術造就之，不用他道，盖與二帝、三之時同。彼漢文、景猶未能罷黜百家、表章六經；唐終其祚，常以詩賦取材；宋仁宗以後乃用經義，而濂、洛所明者尚見擯棄也，豈若今用儒之純哉！用之純者，得效必大且久。以臣觀之，每科必有傑然偉人，如亘天
translation_en: … the sacred decision of His Majesty, which is an increase in number compared to previous examinations. Their surnames and personal names, along with their essays, are engraved in print, respectfully submitted above to occupy His Majesty's late-night perusal, and presented below to serve as a model for scholars who carry on learning. Your servant [Liu] Dingzhi 刘定之 bows and prostrates himself, saying: Our August Dynasty has selected scholars to exalt a prosperous and harmonious era for over a hundred years now, molding them all through Confucian learning without resorting to other doctrines; indeed, this is the same as in the times of the Two Emperors and Three [Kings] [? 三 missing 王]. Even under Emperors Wen and Jing of the Han, they were not yet able to dismiss the Hundred Schools and venerate the Six Classics; the Tang, throughout its reign, regularly selected talent by means of poetry and rhapsodies; and in the Song, only from Emperor Renzong onward did they employ essays on the meaning of the Classics, yet what had been elucidated by the masters of Lian and Luo was still rejected and cast aside. How could any of those compare to the purity with which Confucianism is employed today! When it is employed with purity, the results achieved are bound to be great and enduring. As your servant observes it, in every examination cohort there are bound to be outstandingly great men, just as across the sky…

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
繁星必有芒寒色正以緯耀
經者焉諸俊乂由茲以對
廷立
朝建功樹業豈無仰助我
皇上鞏固太平萬億載之圖者乎
主司將賴之曰此亦微臣之
所以報
===
國以少逭尸素之咎者也又以
自附於陸贄之能得韓愈歐
陽脩之能得蘇軾轍也豈不
與有榮耀垂竹帛哉是庸序
諸簡端
中順大夫太常寺少卿兼翰
林院侍讀學士劉定之謹序
alt_text:
繁星必有益寔色正以緯耀
經者焉諸俊乂由茲以對
廷立
朝建功樹業豈無仰助我
皇上鞏固太平萬億載之圖者乎
主司將賴之曰此亦微臣之
所以報
===
國以少逭尸素之咎者也又以
自附於陸贄之能得韓愈歐
陽脩之能得蘇軾轍也豈不
與有榮耀垂竹帛哉是庸序
諸簡端
中順大夫太常寺少卿兼翰
林院侍讀學士劉定之謹序
punctuated:
繁星，必有芒寒色正以緯耀經者焉。諸俊乂由茲以對廷立朝，建功樹業，豈無仰助我皇上鞏固太平萬億載之圖者乎？主司將賴之曰：「此亦微臣之所以報國，以少逭尸素之咎者也；又以自附於陸贄之能得韓愈、歐陽脩之能得蘇軾、轍也。」豈不與有榮耀、垂竹帛哉？是庸序諸簡端。
中順大夫、太常寺少卿兼翰林院侍讀學士劉定之謹序。
translation_en:
… myriad stars, among which there are surely those of chill radiance and pure hue that illuminate the warp as the woof. When all these men of outstanding talent proceed from here to respond at the Palace Examination and take their stand at court, establishing achievements and building great enterprises, how could there fail to be those who look up to assist Our August Emperor in consolidating his grand design of Great Peace for a myriad myriad years? The examiners will rely upon them and say: "This is also whereby we humble servants repay the state and slightly escape the blame of holding office idly without merit; and whereby we may attach ourselves to the likes of Lu Zhi 陸贄 in being able to obtain Han Yu 韓愈, and Ouyang Xiu 歐陽脩 in being able to obtain Su Shi 蘇軾 and Su Zhe 蘇轍." Will they not share in the glory and have their names handed down on bamboo and silk? For this reason I write this preface at the head of the pages.

Respectfully prefaced by Liu Dingzhi 劉定之, Grand Master forThe Courteous Compliance, Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices concurrently Expositor-in-Waiting in the Hanlin Academy.

translation_en:

第壹塲

四書
《詩》云：「邦畿千里，惟民所止。」《詩》云：「緡蠻黄鳥，止于丘隅。」子曰：「於止，知其所止，可以人而不如鳥乎？」《詩》云：「穆穆文王，於緝熈敬止。」為人君，止於仁；為人臣，止於敬；為人子，止於孝；為人父，止於慈；與國人交，止於信。
為之難，言之得無訒乎？
禹惡旨酒而好善言。湯執中，立賢無方。文王視民如傷，望道而未之見。武王不泄邇，不忘遠。周公思兼三王，以施四事；其有不合者，仰而思之，夜以繼日；幸而得之，坐以待旦。

進以正，可以正邦也。

translation_en:
First Session

Four Books
1. The Book of Odes (Shi) says: "The royal domain of a thousand li is where the people rest." The Book of Odes says: "The twittering yellow bird rests on a corner of the mound." The Master said: "In resting, it knows where to rest. Can a human being not be the equal of a bird?" The Book of Odes says: "Profound was King Wen; oh, how continuously bright and reverent was his resting!" As a ruler, he rested in benevolence; as a minister, he rested in reverence; as a son, he rested in filial piety; as a father, he rested in kindness; in dealings with the people of the state, he rested in trustworthiness.
2. Doing it is difficult; in speaking of it, can one avoid being hesitant?
3. Yu hated fine wine and loved good words. Tang held fast to the Mean and established the worthy without regard to their origins. King Wen looked upon the people as if they were wounded, and gazed toward the Way as if he had not yet seen it. King Wu did not treat those near him with familiarity and did not forget those who were distant. The Duke of Zhou sought to combine the achievements of the Three Kings in order to carry out the four undertakings; when there was anything that did not fit, he looked up and thought about it, from night into day; and when by good fortune he grasped it, he sat waiting for the dawn.

Book of Changes (Yi)
1. The gentleman practices these four virtues; therefore it is said: "Qian: originating, flourishing, advantageous, and firm."
2. Advancing with rectitude, one can rectify the state.
3. It encompasses the transformations of heaven and earth without erring; it intricately brings the myriad things to completion without leaving anything out; …

"They are brought into order in Xun. Xun is the southeast; 'brought into order' means that all things are clean and orderly. Li means brightness, in which all things are visible to one another; it is the trigram of the south."

Book of Documents (Shu)
"Rest in your proper stopping place; attend to the subtle springs of things, and so secure peace."
"The great God on high has conferred a moral sense upon the people below. Compliance with their constant nature, and the ability to make them tranquil in their course, belong solely to the sovereign."
"When our people guide their youths, let them cherish the products of the soil, and their hearts will be good. Let them listen attentively to the constant instructions of their ancestors and fathers; as to virtues, small and great, let the youths treat them as one. People of the land of Mei, hereafter ply your limbs and devote yourselves wholly to cultivating millet, hastening about to serve your fathers and elders. Lead forth your oxen and carts to engage in trade afar, so as to filially support your parents. Then your parents will rejoice, and you may wash the vessels cleanly and set forth rich food, offering wine for use."
"I have heard that in ancient times, when Cheng Tang had received the Mandate, he had at that time a minister like Yi Yin, whose attainment reached to August Heaven. Under Tai Jia, there was at that time one like the Protector and Regulator (Baoheng). Under Tai Wu, there were at that time men like Yi Zhi and Chen Hu, whose attainment reached to God on High, while Wu Xian regulated the royal house."

text:
文章獨詳焉非特以其世年近而易知
著多也尤以其為時王制作所當遵也
故其言曰吾從周他人之言之者曰憲
章文武仰惟我
祖宗所以垂訓天下後世則有書矣大誥中褒
善之言藹乎春溫也善之著者誰歟貶
惡之辭肅乎秋殺也惡之尤者誰歟何

translation_en: …and institutions of the former kings of Zhou in particular detail? It was not merely because their era was recent, making them easy to know and record at length, but especially because they were the creations of the reigning dynasty and ought to be followed. Thus he said, "I follow Zhou," and others speaking of him said, "He modeled himself on the regulations of Kings Wen and Wu." Looking up with reverence to how Our Imperial Ancestors handed down instructions for the Empire and posterity, there are books for this. In the Grand Pronouncements (Da gao), the words praising goodness are as genial as the warmth of spring—who were those most notable for goodness? The expressions censuring evil are as stern as the blight of autumn—who were the most egregious in evil? Which chapters share the same purport as the Record of Filial and Obedient Deeds (Xiaoshun shishi), and among the ancients who rose to the highest ministerial offices through their filial obedience, who is the most illustrious? Which chapters share the same meaning as the Hidden Rewards of Doing Good (Weishan yinzhi), and among the ancients whose hidden virtue brought blessings flowing down to their descendants, who is the most prominent? The Book of the Five Human Relationships (Wulun shu) records not only antiquity, but also the present age. Among the various officials who lived to serve Our Imperial Ancestors, in the civil service who was the most incorruptible and upright, and in the military service who achieved the greatest merit? Now, if scholars who wear the student's collar and girdle pendants merely search far back into the texts of high antiquity while neglecting near at hand the regulations of our illustrious dynasty, this is contrary to the intent of what Confucius followed and modeled himself upon—and how could that be permissible? Let each of you cite and discuss the general outlines of these several books, in the hope that it may suffice to show that you have paid attention to them in the past, and that today, in your aspiration to be of service to the world, one may also recognize that you take encouragement and warning from them so as to remain free from delusion. Would this not…

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
世道有補哉
問先儒謂孟子之書象論語盖大賢擬聖
而作也其旨意宜無不同焉者竊嘗考
之有不同者多矣姑舉一二與諸士講
之孔子君命召不俟駕敬君命禮也而
孟子將朝聞命遂不果於禮何在歟孔
子去衞明日遂行去他國道也而孟子
去齊三宿然後出晝於道何在歟孔子
不許原憲辭常祿義也而孟子為上卿
===
竟不受齊祿義又何處歟孔子曰樂則
韶舞取其盡善盡美也孟子曰今之樂
猶古之樂何獨不取韶樂歟孔子曰畏
大人是教人修己有所畏也孟子曰說
大人則藐之何又教人以不畏歟孔子
遭阨于匡人則曰文王既沒文不在兹
是取必於己也孟子見沮於臧氏則曰
不遇魯侯天也何又取必於天歟其有
不同焉者多類此安在其為擬聖而作

punctuated:
世道有補哉？
問：先儒謂《孟子》之書象《論語》，盖大賢擬聖而作也，其旨意宜無不同焉者。竊嘗考之，有不同者多矣，姑舉一二與諸士講之。孔子君命召，不俟駕，敬君命，禮也；而孟子將朝，聞命遂不果，於禮何在歟？孔子去衞，明日遂行，去他國，道也；而孟子去齊，三宿然後出晝，於道何在歟？孔子不許原憲辭常祿，義也；而孟子為上卿，竟不受齊祿，義又何處歟？孔子曰「樂則《韶》《舞》」，取其盡善盡美也；孟子曰「今之樂猶古之樂」，何獨不取《韶》樂歟？孔子曰「畏大人」，是教人修己有所畏也；孟子曰「說大人則藐之」，何又教人以不畏歟？孔子遭阨于匡人，則曰「文王既沒，文不在兹」，是取必於己也；孟子見沮於臧氏，則曰「不遇魯侯，天也」，何又取必於天歟？其有不同焉者多類此，安在其為擬聖而作…
translation_en:
…be of benefit to the ways of the world?

Question: Former Confucians said that the book of the Mencius (Mengzi) resembles the Analects (Lunyu), having been composed by a great worthy in emulation of the Sage, and that its purport and meaning ought to have nothing in which they differ. Yet when I have privately examined them, there are many points where they differ. Let me tentatively raise one or two of them to discuss with you gentlemen. When Confucius was summoned by his ruler's command, he went without waiting for his carriage to be yoked; respecting the ruler's command is ritual propriety. Yet when Mencius was about to go to court, upon hearing the king's summons he did not carry through with it—where in this is ritual propriety? When Confucius left Wei, he departed the very next day; such is the Way of leaving another state. Yet when Mencius left Qi, he lodged for three nights before leaving Zhou—where in this is the Way? Confucius did not allow Yuan Xian to decline his regular emolument, which was rightness; yet Mencius served as a Senior Minister and in the end did not accept the emolument of Qi—how was rightness handled here? Confucius said, "For music, take the Shao dances," choosing them for being both utterly felicitous and utterly paragonal; Mencius said, "Today's music is like the music of antiquity"—why did he alone not choose the Shao music? Confucius said, "Stand in awe of great men," which teaches people to hold something in awe in cultivating themselves; Mencius said, "When speaking to great men, look upon them as small"—why did he instead teach people not to stand in awe? When Confucius met with distress from the people of Kuang, he said, "Now that King Wen is dead, is not culture lodged here in me?"—thus staking certainty upon himself. When Mencius was thwarted by the Zang clan, he said, "That I did not meet the Lord of Lu is due to Heaven"—why did he instead stake certainty upon Heaven? The points where they differ are mostly of this sort; how then can it be considered a work composed in emulation of the Sage…

此必嘗玩索而有得矣其詳悉以對

則有之非外物也故凡委質為臣者不
可一日而不忠考之往古賢臣能盡忠

punctuated:
者乎？諸士誦孔孟之書，學孔孟之學，於此必嘗玩索而有得矣，其詳悉以對。

問：先儒曰：「忠，人之義也，猶耳目心腹，有身則有之，非外物也。」故凡委質為臣者，不可一日而不忠。考之往古，賢臣能盡忠君之道者，鮮有不受忠君之名；然亦有受名於時，而不能無他瑕疵議者，試與諸士論之。如身都保傅，不能弭流言之毀，何以號為「上忠」？□居宰父，不能逃小器之譏，何以號為「次忠」歟？有起自隴西，其明珠文犀之謗似貪矣，若何得謚「忠成」？起自隆中，其食少事煩之誚似迂矣，若何得謚「忠武」歟？累罷累復，而俛首以事偽周，似苟容矣，于何褒曰「忠正」？屢相屢出，而不能厲志以復河朔，似無謀矣，于何褒曰「文忠」歟？羽書五至，人孰不駭，可謂急矣，而何飲笑自如，天下稱為「大度」？執政三朝，或病其專，可謂危矣，而□□□
translation_en:
… [written in imitation of the Sage]? You gentlemen recite the books of Confucius and Mencius and study the learning of Confucius and Mencius; you must have pondered and explored these matters and gained insight into them. Answer in full detail.

Question: A former Confucian scholar said: "Loyalty is a person's duty; like the ears, eyes, heart, and belly, if one has a body one possesses them—it is not an external thing." Therefore, anyone who pledges himself to serve as a minister cannot go a single day without being loyal. Examining antiquity, among worthy ministers who were able to exhaust the Way of loyalty to their ruler, few failed to receive a reputation for loyalty to their ruler; yet there were also those who received such a reputation in their time, while not being free of other flaws or criticisms[?]. Let us discuss them with you gentlemen. For example, one personally held the offices of Protector and Tutor (Baofu 保傅, i.e., the Duke of Zhou 周公), yet could not stop the slander of rumors—how then was he styled "Supreme Loyalty" (Shangzhong 上忠)? Another occupied the position of Chief Minister and "Father" [仲父, i.e., Guan Zhong 管仲], yet could not escape the ridicule of being a vessel of small capacity—how then was he styled "Next in Loyalty" (Cizhong 次忠)? There was one who rose from Longxi 隴西 (i.e., Ma Yuan 馬援), for whom the slander about bright pearls and patterned rhinoceros horn seemed like greed—how did he obtain the posthumous title "Loyal and Accomplished" (Zhongcheng 忠成, [sic, 忠成/忠誠])? And one who rose from Longzhong 隆中 (i.e., Zhuge Liang 諸葛亮), for whom the taunt of "eating little while attending to繁 many affairs" seemed impractical—how did he obtain the posthumous title "Loyal and Martial" (Zhongwu 忠武)? One was repeatedly dismissed and repeatedly restored, bowing his head to serve the usurping Zhou dynasty (i.e., Di Renjie 狄仁傑 or Lou Shide 婁師德 / Yao Chong 姚崇)—that seemed like spineless accommodation; why was he praised as "Loyal and Upright" (Zhongzheng 忠正)? Another repeatedly served as Grand Councilor and was repeatedly sent out to the provinces, yet could not rouse his resolve to recover Heshuo 河朔 (i.e., Pei Du 裴度)—that seemed like lacking strategy; why was he praised as "Cultured and Loyal" (Wenzhong 文忠)? When feathered dispatches arrived five times, who would not be alarmed? The situation could be called urgent indeed—yet why did one drink and laugh with composure, so that the empire稱 praised him as "Magnanimous" (Dadu 大度, i.e.,寇準 Kou Zhun / 謝安 Xie An)? Another held the reins of government through three reigns (i.e., Han Qi 韓琦), and some faulted him for monopolizing power; his position could be called perilous indeed—yet [despite obstacles he did not…?]…

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
阻不避天下稱爲忠勇然數君子之迹
具在簡冊有可考者諸士拜官涖事指
日可俟矣果以何人爲法歟抑其間有
不足法者歟願明言之以觀尚友之學
問邇者
皇上臨辟雝以造士宜乎士務學問而夙成矣
耕藉田以勸農宜乎農力稼穡而歲豐矣奈
何庠序猶淹而至限年四十以拔之饑
饉相仍而至遣使再出以賑之蓋在下
===
奉承者之未至以致然也如是則教育
之方救荒之政今也何施而可若乃官
不修其職而恣肆於郡縣三載之
覲汰去亦多矣民不奠其居而弄兵於潢池
數年之間殄殲亦衆矣然安得繼此莫
不爲循良之歸而前召父後杜母莫不
懷革面之誠而賣刀劒買牛犢乎如是
則守令之選盜賊之弭今也何由而宜
夫爲治所當注意者無過於士有成材

punctuated:
阻不避，天下稱爲忠勇。然數君子之迹，具在簡冊，有可考者。諸士拜官涖事，指日可俟矣，果以何人爲法歟？抑其間有不足法者歟？願明言之，以觀尚友之學。
問：邇者皇上臨辟雝以造士，宜乎士務學問而夙成矣；耕藉田以勸農，宜乎農力稼穡而歲豐矣。奈何庠序猶淹，而至限年四十以拔之；饑饉相仍，而至遣使再出以賑之？蓋在下奉承者之未至，以致然也。如是，則教育之方、救荒之政，今也何施而可？若乃官不修其職，而恣肆於郡縣，三載之覲，汰去亦多矣；民不奠其居，而弄兵於潢池，數年之間，殄殲亦衆矣。然安得繼此莫不爲循良之歸，而前召父、後杜母；莫不懷革面之誠，而賣刀劒、買牛犢乎？如是，則守令之選、盜賊之弭，今也何由而宜？夫爲治所當注意者，無過於士有成材、
translation_en:
…shirked no obstacles, and the world praised him as loyal and courageous. Yet the deeds of these several gentlemen are all recorded in the historical annals and can be examined. You scholars can expect within days to receive official appointments and assume your duties. Whom, indeed, will you take as your model? Or are there some among them who are not worthy of emulation? Please state this clearly, so that we may observe your learning in befriending the ancients.

Question: Recently, His Majesty visited the Imperial University (Biyong) to cultivate scholars, so it ought to be that scholars devote themselves to learning and reach maturity early; he plowed the Sacred Field (jitian) to encourage agriculture, so it ought to be that farmers exert themselves in sowing and reaping and the harvests are abundant. Why is it, then, that students in the schools still languish, to the point that an age limit of forty had to be set for selecting them; and that famines have followed one upon another, to the point that envoys had to be dispatched a second time to relieve them? This is surely because those below who carry out His Majesty's intentions have fallen short, thus bringing things to this pass. Such being the case, what methods of education and what policies of famine relief can be implemented today? As for officials failing to fulfill their duties and acting wantonly in the prefectures and counties, during the triennial audiences many have already been weeded out; and as for the common people failing to remain settled in their homes and taking up arms in rebellion ("playing with weapons in the decorative pool"), over the course of several years many have been exterminated. Yet how can we ensure that hereafter all officials turn into models of upright and benevolent administration, like "Father Shao before and Mother Du after," and that all rebels cherish a sincere change of heart, selling their swords and blades to buy oxen and calves? Such being the case, by what means today can the selection of prefects and magistrates and the pacification of bandits and rebels be properly accomplished? Now, among the things to which governance ought to pay heed, nothing surpasses scholars becoming accomplished talents,…

translation_en:
…that farmers have surplus grain, officials provide good governance, and the common people possess settled resolve. [?] His Majesty on the throne labors from before dawn until late at night planning solely for these ends, and all those at Court likewise strive to fulfill His virtuous intentions. Therefore, I broadly inquire of and consult you assembled men of talent, trusting that you will surely have a full account to offer on these matters.

Question: Since antiquity, there has never been a lack of men to defend against the northern and western barbarians (Rong and Di). Wei Qing 衛青 and Huo Q病霍去病 were originally menial servants, yet they struck the Xiongnu and won repeated victories—by what capability was this achieved? Han Qi 韓琦 and Fan Zhongyan 范仲淹 were originally Confucian scholars, yet they pressed Yuanhao 元昊 (Nangxiao 曩霄) into submitting as a subject—by what strategy was this accomplished? How [?] it was to excavate a field and play kickball beyond the desert! How lax in precautions it was to have an assassin take a belt from inside one's bedchamber! How arbitrary and overstepping it was to [?]! And how rash it was to exchange correspondence with rebellious bandits! Yet in the end they achieved success through these actions; there must have been a reason. Today, the northern nomads (Hu) are arrogant in the north and the Qiang are cunning in the west; those who hold the battle-axes of command are noble scions and those who grasp strategic authority come from hereditary military families, yet their achievements put them to shame before the men of antiquity. Shall we then make peace with the Chanyu? One fears we would still not avoid having to inspect the troops at Xiliu; why then did those worthy ministers of the Han advise making peace as their counsel? Shall we form a covenant with the Tibetans (Tubo)? One fears suffering a treacherous ambush like that at Qingshui; why then did those fine generals of the Tang request a covenant? As for the art of war: the Five Formations of Xuanyuan (the Yellow Emperor) were rooted in the Five Phases (wuxing), and the Eight Formations of Kongming (Zhuge Liang 諸葛亮) were rooted in the Eight Trigrams (bagua). The variations in their configurations…

punctuated: 之變、方向之殊，固為將者之所當素講。而洙泗之教曰「有文事必有武備」，其可以不強學待問乎？尚備著于篇，得其說者將以獻焉。惟皇上方弘將將之畧，倘有取於萬一，亦芹曝之誠所由達也。
translation_en: …transformation of their dispositions and the differences in their orientations are indeed what a commander ought to have studied thoroughly beforehand. Moreover, the teachings of the Zhu and Si rivers [i.e., Confucius] state that "whoever has civil affairs must also have military preparations"; how could one fail to study strenuously in anticipation of being questioned? Set forth your views fully in your essay, and those whose explanations succeed shall be presented. Considering that His Majesty the Emperor is just now expanding his grand strategy for commanding commanders, should even one part in ten thousand be adopted, it will also be the means by which your humble and sincere devotion is conveyed.

四書

The Four Books

text:
人之所當止者也然非大賢兩引詩而以聖人
之言明於前一引詩而以聖人之止實於後抑
何以知其然哉思昔曾子　　　　三章釋止
至善之義而引商頌玄鳥之詩言王畿千里之
廣大林林之民止於是揔揔之眾居於是以明
物各有所止也又引小雅綿蠻之詩言綿蠻和
聲之黃鳥非無幽谷可棲而必止於丘隅非無
平林可安而必止於岑蔚孔子說之曰黃鳥乃

乎以言人當知所止也夫既觀於物類而知至
善之當止矣豈可不觀於聖人而法至善之當
止乎於是引大雅文王之詩言穆穆深遠之文
王繼續光明而能無不敬以安於所止遂申言

Yet if the Great Worthy had not first twice quoted the Odes (Shi) and elucidated them with the words of the Sage, and afterward once quoted the Odes and substantiated it with the abiding of the Sage, how indeed could one know this to be so? Consider how in the past Master Zeng (Zengzi), in the third chapter of commentary, explained the meaning of "abiding in the highest good" by quoting the ode "Xuan niao" (Dark Bird) from the Sacrificial Odes of Shang (Shang song), speaking of how in the vastness of the royal domain of a thousand li, the teeming people abide therein and the thronging multitudes dwell therein, in order to make clear that all things each have where they abide. He also quoted the ode "Mianman" (Twittering) from the Lesser Odes (Xiao ya), speaking of how the orioles with their twittering harmonious voices are not without dark valleys in which to perch, yet insist on abiding in the corner of a wooded hill; they are not without level forests in which to rest, yet insist on abiding in high, dense foliage. Confucius explained this, saying: "The oriole is but a tiny creature, yet even so, regarding the place where it abides, it knows where to abide; how much more so with man, who is the most sentient of the myriad things—can it be that regarding the good in which he abides, he does not know where to abide?" This was to say that man ought to know where to abide. Now, having observed the categories of creatures and known that one ought to abide in the highest good, how could one not observe the Sage and take as one's model the highest good in which one ought to abide? Thereupon he quoted the ode "Wen Wang" (King Wen) from the Greater Odes (Da ya), speaking of how the profound and far-reaching King Wen continuously maintained his bright virtue, and was able in all things to be reverent so as to rest securely in where he abided. He then went on to state in detail the specific items of where he abided, saying: As a ruler of men, King Wen abided in benevolence; as a subject, he abided in reverence—observing how he showed kindness to the destitute, widowers, and widows, and how he served the Yin dynasty, this can be seen. As a son, King Wen abided in filial piety; as a father, he abided in parental kindness—observing how he paid court to King Ji and was able to instruct King Wu, this can be seen. 易則其言豈得而易哉昔夫子答司馬牛之問

translation_en:
For speaking is not difficult, it is acting that is difficult; since the humane person constantly preserves his mind and does not take action lightly, how then could his speech be facile? In the past, when the Master answered Sima Niu's question about humaneness, it was as if he said: "It is only because a person's mind is lost that he follows his whims and acts recklessly; it is only because his actions are reckless that he speaks unrestrainedly and without scruple. The humane person is not like this. His mind is not fettered like a lost chicken or dog, nor does it gallop off after thoughts of wild swans. Therefore, when he is about to do something, he is cautious and wary as if holding jade or carrying a full vessel, fearing only that he might be careless and make a mistake; when he is about to carry something out, he is trembling with awe as if approaching a deep abyss or treading on thin ice, worried only that he might beremiss and incur some blame. Since doing it is as difficult as this, how could he allow himself to speak of it lightly? Therefore, in speaking he must consider how it will end; even though he need not seal his mouth three times, he naturally cannot help being hesitant in speech—how could he go so far as to commit the absurdity of excessive facility? In speaking he must take account of his actions; even though he need not thrice repeat the lines on the flaw in the white jade tablet, he naturally cannot help being slow to speak—how could he go so far as to commit the rambling of excessive prolixity? Thus, being hesitant in his speech is precisely what constitutes humaneness; how could that Sima Niu treat it lightly?" Alas! Hesitancy in speech is not enough to exhaust the meaning of humaneness, yet the words of a humane person naturally do not come forth lightly; for although this is not the entirety of humaneness, it is nevertheless one aspect of its virtue. title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
聞伯益之昌言則好而拜之成湯有商聖王也於
中道則執之而不失於賢才則立之而無方禹
湯何如其心哉丕顯者文王也民已安矣而視
之如有傷道已至矣而望之若未見丕承者武
王也迩者人泄之而已則不泄遠者人忘之而
己則不忘文武何如其心哉禹也湯也其事不
同也周公則思兼乎禹湯而行其事文也武也
其事不一也周公則思兼乎文武而施其事然
古今異宜事不能以皆合彼此殊勢事不能以
===
不異故仰以致其思至於夜以繼日而思之切
焉幸而得其理又必坐以待旦而行之急焉是
則周公之心即三王之心三王之心即周公之
心其為憂勤惕厲曷甞以古今而有間哉嗟夫
天理常存人心不泯符契若合関百聖而如一
人統緒相承歷萬古而如一日故孟子於前章
言舜此章言禹湯文武周公而後此二章又言
孔子而以己繼之道統之傳端可見矣

punctuated: 聞伯益之昌言，則好而拜之。成湯，有商聖王也。於中道則執之而不失，於賢才則立之而無方。禹、湯何如其心哉！丕顯者，文王也。民已安矣，而視之如有傷；道已至矣，而望之若未見。丕承者，武王也。迩者人泄之，而已則不泄；遠者人忘之，而已則不忘。文、武何如其心哉！禹也，湯也，其事不同也，周公則思兼乎禹、湯而行其事；文也，武也，其事不一也，周公則思兼乎文、武而施其事。然古今異宜，事不能以皆合；彼此殊勢，事不能以不異。故仰以致其思，至於夜以繼日，而思之切焉；幸而得其理，又必坐以待旦，而行之急焉。是則周公之心，即三王之心；三王之心，即周公之心。其為憂勤惕厲，曷甞以古今而有間哉！嗟夫！天理常存，人心不泯。符契若合，関百聖而如一人；統緒相承，歷萬古而如一日。故孟子於前章言舜，此章言禹、湯、文、武、周公，而後此二章又言孔子，而以己繼之，道統之傳，端可見矣。
translation_en: …when he heard the admirable words of Boyi 伯益, he loved them and bowed to them. Cheng Tang 成湯 was the sage-king of the Shang. As for the Way of the Mean, he held fast to it without losing it; as for worthy talents, he established them in office without limit. What were the minds of Yu 禹 and Tang 湯 like! Greatly illustrious was King Wen 文王. Though the people were already at peace, he looked upon them as if they were still suffering; though the Way had already reached its perfection, he gazed toward it as if he had not yet seen it. Greatly continuing the work was King Wu 武王. What was near at hand, others treated with familiarity, yet he himself did not treat with familiarity; what was distant, others forgot, yet he himself did not forget. What were the minds of Wen and Wu like! As for Yu and Tang, their deeds were not the same, yet the Duke of Zhou 周公 sought to combine the ways of Yu and Tang and carry out their deeds; as for Wen and Wu, their deeds were not uniform, yet the Duke of Zhou sought to combine the ways of Wen and Wu and put their deeds into practice. However, antiquity and the present differ in what is appropriate, so their deeds could not in every case coincide; their respective circumstances varied, so their deeds could not but differ. Therefore, looking up, he applied his thoughts, even continuing from night into day in the earnestness of his reflection; and if by good fortune he grasped the principle, he would sit waiting for the dawn in his urgency to put it into action. Thus the mind of the Duke of Zhou was none other than the mind of the Three Kings, and the mind of the Three Kings was none other than the mind of the Duke of Zhou. In their anxious diligence and vigilant awe, how could there ever be any gap between antiquity and the present! Alas! Heavenly principle endures forever, and the human mind is never extinguished. Matching like the two halves of a tally, it spans a hundred sages as though they were a single person; the lineage of the Way is handed down in succession, passing through ten thousand ages as though they were a single day. Thus Mencius 孟子 in the preceding chapter spoke of Shun 舜, in this chapter speaks of Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, and the Duke of Zhou, and in the two chapters following this speaks again of Confucius 孔子, continuing the line with himself—the transmission of the succession of the Way (daotong 道統) can truly be seen here.

When sovereign and minister are of one mind, and those above and below are united in rectitude, then within the royal court, the hundred officials can be rectified without any trend toward partiality or selfishness; and throughout the realm within the seas, the myriad people can be rectified without any custom of depravity or perversity. In the rectitude of his virtue, he condescends to share it with his great ministers; in the centrality of his virtue, he rises preeminent above the multitude of things. At such a time, the flourishing of transformative governance relies entirely upon the great sovereign of the Nine in the Fifth Place who embodies centrality and rectitude. Oh, how magnificent!

…east of due south—this is the position of the trigram Xun. Because its position is here, things that previously were not yet clean and even now become clean and even. Thus, what is curved sprouts forth and what is shelled splits open—how sleek and bright is their cleanliness! What is womb-born breathes and what is egg-born takes wing—how orderly is their even gathering! When the Sage speaks thus of Xun in the Later Heaven arrangement, is this not citing the position of the trigram to explain its meaning? And why is it said that "they become visible to one another in Li"? One should observe this in the virtue of the trigram Li. Li represents the sun, and the image of the sun is great brightness; Li represents summer, and the season of summer is yang brightness—this is the virtue of Li. Because its virtue is such, things that previously had not yet become visible to one another now become visible to one another. Thus, form in its own form and color in its own color, shining brightly upon one another, take place amid the summer transformations in the south associated with the trigram Li; flying in the clouds and swimming in the streams, resplendently beholding one another, take place during the time of the warm southern winds associated with the trigram Li. When the Sage speaks thus of Li in the Later Heaven arrangement, is this not citing the virtue of the trigram to discuss its position? Even so, there is the Changes of the Former Heaven and there is the Changes of the Later Heaven. What the preceding chapter says from "thunder rouses them, wind scatters them" onward is the Former Heaven Changes of mutual opposition; what this chapter says from "they come forth in Zhen, they are made even in Xun" onward is the Later Heaven Changes of cyclical progression. Without mutual opposition, cyclical progression has nothing by which to establish its substance; without cyclical progression, mutual opposition has nothing by which to carry out its function. The Changes of Fuxi and the Changes of King Wen can exist together and cannot do without each other—how could one allow them to be sundered into two?

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
萬化之原也欲謹其身之所居可不安其心之
所止乎彼心之德仁也仁固吾心之所止吾則
順適乎仁而不杌隉於外誘心之制義也義亦
吾心之所止吾則順適乎義而不搖奪於私欲
視聽言動一循乎理好惡用舍不違乎天如是
則心安所止固足為萬事之樞紐矣而應事之
際又可不究於心乎彼事之發也有善焉有未
善焉於是極深研幾圖難於其易為大於其細
必求其善而後已事之著也有安焉有未安焉
===
於是熟思審處不輕於有為不幸於苟成必適
於安而後已惟幾所以謹其始惟康所以憲其
其終如是則事皆合理而心之所止益無不安
矣吁靜而安乎心事之本以立動而謹乎事心
之用以行動靜交養體用兼全謹位之道孰有
要於此哉雖然惟精惟一允執厥中舜之止已
安矣惟時惟幾庶事康哉舜於事已審矣而大
禹猶以是告不亦瀆乎盖大禹不以其君既聖
而忘責難之恭帝舜亦不以治功已成而忘謹

punctuated: 萬化之原也。欲謹其身之所居，可不安其心之所止乎？彼心之德，仁也；仁固吾心之所止，吾則順適乎仁，而不杌隉於外誘。心之制，義也；義亦吾心之所止，吾則順適乎義，而不搖奪於私欲。視聽言動，一循乎理；好惡用舍，不違乎天。如是，則心安所止，固足為萬事之樞紐矣。而應事之際，又可不究於心乎？彼事之發也，有善焉，有未善焉，於是極深研幾，圖難於其易，為大於其細，必求其善而後已。事之著也，有安焉，有未安焉，於是熟思審處，不輕於有為，不幸於苟成，必適於安而後已。惟幾，所以謹其始；惟康，所以憲其其終。如是，則事皆合理，而心之所止益無不安矣。吁！靜而安乎心，事之本以立；動而謹乎事，心之用以行。動靜交養，體用兼全，謹位之道，孰有要於此哉？雖然，「惟精惟一，允執厥中」，舜之止已安矣；「惟時惟幾，庶事康哉」，舜於事已審矣。而大禹猶以是告，不亦瀆乎？盖大禹不以其君既聖而忘責難之恭，帝舜亦不以治功已成而忘謹
translation_en:
…is the source of all transformations. If a ruler wishes to exercise care in the position he occupies, can he fail to settle his mind where it should abide? The virtue of the mind is benevolence. Since benevolence is indeed where my mind should abide, I conform to benevolence and am not unsettled by external enticements. What governs the mind is righteousness. Since righteousness too is where my mind should abide, I conform to righteousness and am not swayed or overcome by selfish desires. In seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting, I follow principle throughout; in liking and disliking, employing and dismissing, I do not depart from Heaven. Thus the mind rests securely where it should abide and is fully capable of serving as the pivot of all affairs. Yet when responding to affairs, can one fail to examine them thoroughly in one's mind? When affairs first arise, some are good and some are not yet good. One therefore probes their depths and investigates their incipient tendencies, plans for difficulties while they are still easy, and undertakes great things while they are still small, never resting until one has attained what is good. When affairs become manifest, some are settled and some are not yet settled. One therefore reflects thoroughly and deals with them judiciously, neither acting rashly nor hoping for success through makeshift measures, never resting until a satisfactory resolution is reached. Attending to incipient tendencies is how one exercises care at the beginning; attending to well-being is how one regulates their outcome [?]. Thus all affairs accord with principle, and the mind becomes ever more securely settled wherever it should abide.

Ah! In stillness, settling the mind establishes the foundation of affairs; in activity, attending carefully to affairs brings the mind's functioning into effect. Activity and stillness nourish each other, and substance and function are both fully realized. In the way of exercising care in one's position, what could be more essential than this? Nevertheless, through being “discerning and single-minded, sincerely holding fast to the mean,” Shun was already secure in where his mind abided; through “attending to timeliness and incipient tendencies, so that all affairs might prosper,” Shun was already judicious in his handling of affairs. Yet Yu the Great still admonished him in these terms. Was this not importunate? It was because Yu the Great did not forget the respect expressed in demanding difficult things of his ruler merely because that ruler was already a sage; nor did Emperor Shun, because his achievements in government were already complete, forget to exercise care…

自克夏誕誥萬方本上天生民之理見在己君

translation_en: …could one make the people abide peacefully in their Way and preserve intact their constant nature? In antiquity, when Cheng Tang returned from conquering Xia and issued a grand announcement to the myriad regions, he grounded his words in the principle by which High Heaven gives birth to the people in order to show the gravity of the Way of the ruler that rested upon himself. His meaning was to say: The August Supreme Di gives birth to the people below; with vital force (qi) their physical form is constituted, and principle (li) is likewise endowed in them. Benevolence and righteousness are none other than the principles sent down by the Supreme Di, originally without a single hair's breadth of partiality or leaning; propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness are likewise none other than the principles sent down by the Supreme Di, originally without a single moment's bias or distortion. When people follow their natural benevolence and righteousness, then their constant nature of benevolence and righteousness is naturally no different from when the mandate was first sent down; when they follow their natural propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness, then their constant nature of propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness is naturally no different from when the mandate was first bestowed. Yet although the mandate sent down is the same, the vital force with which people are endowed differs; thus there are cases in which their nature cannot be preserved intact in its natural state, and the Way cannot be practiced as it ought to be. Therefore, on the basis of their nature of benevolence and righteousness, one establishes teachings of benevolence and righteousness, and only then can fathers and sons, rulers and ministers abide peacefully in the Way of benevolence and righteousness as they ought without losing it—this lies in the office of the one who rules All under Heaven. On the basis of their nature of propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness, one establishes teachings of propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness, and only then can elders and juniors, husbands and wives, and friends abide peacefully in the Way of propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness as they ought without violating it—this lies in the responsibility of the one who rules All under Heaven. This being so, in possessing All under Heaven today, how could one fail to fulfill the Way of being a ruler and betray the charge of High Heaven? Moreover, if we examine Zhong Hui's counsel to Cheng Tang, it says, "Heaven gives birth to the people with desires." Yet here Cheng Tang speaks instead of their "having a constant nature"—why is this? It is because Zhong Hui based his words on…

…feelings to speak of people's desires, and without a ruler there is no means to restrain those desires; Cheng Tang traced back to innate nature to clarify people's goodness, and without a ruler there is no means to guide that goodness. The discussions of the sage and the worthy illuminate one another—how could they be anything other than stating that the Way of the ruler is of such great importance to all under Heaven!

"Our people guided their youths to cherish only the products of the soil, so their hearts would be good; to listen attentively to the constant instructions of their grandfathers and fathers; and toward great and small virtues alike, that the youths should regard them as one. People of the land of Mei, hereafter ply your limbs and purely cultivate your glutinous and panicled millet; hasten about to serve your fathers and your elders; diligently lead your carts and oxen afar to engage in trade, thereby filially nourishing your parents. When your parents rejoice, you may yourselves wash the vessels clean and set forth rich offerings, bringing out wine for use."

Zhang Hai 張海
Comment by Associate Examiner and Examining Editor Geng 耿: This topic has quite a few threads and is difficult to encompass as a whole. Among the candidates in the examination hall, those who are not overly diffuse are overly sketchy, making them tiresome to read. This essay lays out its narrative in balanced proportions, and its diction is also classical and rich—a fine piece of work.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Junior Compiler Yin 尹: In this piece, the opening sentence of the exposition manages to encompass the whole topic, and the elaboration is also coherent throughout. Compared to other essays that are fragmentary and disorganized, does this one not stand alone in excellence?
Comment by Associate Examiner and Senior Compiler Wang 王: On the topic from the "Announcement about Drunkenness" (Jiu gao 酒誥), candidates in the examination hall were generally able to write essays, yet they were tedious and unsatisfactory. If one seeks an essay as concise and clear as this one, it is rarely seen.

之可取
考試官學士劉批委曲詳盡
聖君既述前王因民訓而申謹酒之戒復以己
意教民孝而開用酒之端盖酒固當謹而用之
亦有道也謹之以遵親之訓用之於孝親之餘
文武聖王教民之意何其兼至哉昔武王欲康
叔明大命於妹邦而告之若曰乃穆考文王肇
國西土訓告其民意謂豈獨我欲謹尓酒哉我
===
民之父老亦常訓其子以惟種稑之生於土者
是愛而無外慕則善心生而自不迷于麴糵常
導其孫以惟黍粟之出於土者是愛而無外誘
則良心存而自不酣於糟粕尓為子者當聰聽
尓考之常訓不可以謹酒為小德德無大小而
視之惟一焉為孫者當明聽尓祖之彜訓不可
以謹酒為小善善無大小而視之無二焉文王
謹酒之教如此今尓妹土之民可不知所謹乎
必也嗣尓股肱之力而無怠惰竭尓胼胝之勞

聖君既述前王因民訓而申謹酒之戒，復以己意教民孝而開用酒之端。盖酒固當謹，而用之亦有道也。謹之以遵親之訓，用之於孝親之餘，文、武聖王教民之意，何其兼至哉！昔武王欲康叔明大命於妹邦，而告之若曰：「乃穆考文王肇國西土，訓告其民，意謂豈獨我欲謹尓酒哉？我民之父老，亦常訓其子以惟種稑之生於土者是愛而無外慕，則善心生而自不迷于麴糵；常導其孫以惟黍粟之出於土者是愛而無外誘，則良心存而自不酣於糟粕。尓為子者，當聰聽尓考之常訓，不可以謹酒為小德，德無大小而視之惟一焉；為孫者，當明聽尓祖之彜訓，不可以謹酒為小善，善無大小而視之無二焉。」文王謹酒之教如此，今尓妹土之民，可不知所謹乎？必也嗣尓股肱之力而無怠惰，竭尓胼胝之勞…
translation_en:
Examiner and Academician Wan comments: The diction suffices to convey the meaning of King Wu's proclamation instructing the land of Mei; it is worthy of selection.
Examiner and Academician Liu comments: Thoroughly nuanced and detailed.
The sage ruler, having recounted how the former king drew upon the people's own family instructions to reiterate the admonition to be cautious with wine, goes on from his own intent to teach the people filial piety and thereby open a proper occasion for the use of wine. For while one must indeed be cautious with wine, there is also a proper way to use it. To be cautious with it in obedience to the instructions of one's elders, and to use it after having fulfilled one's filial duties to one's parents—how comprehensive and complete was the intent of the sage kings Wen and Wu in instructing the people! Of old, when King Wu wished Kangshu to make illustrious the great mandate in the land of Mei, he spoke to him to this effect: "Your reverend father King Wen, when founding the state in the western lands, instructed and admonished his people, meaning to say: Is it only I who wish you to be cautious with your wine? The elders among my people also constantly instruct their sons to cherish only the early- and late-ripening grains that grow from the soil without coveting things outside, so that a good heart arises and they naturally do not lose themselves in yeast and malt; they constantly guide their grandsons to cherish only the panicled and glutinous millets that come forth from the soil without being enticed by things outside, so that their innate goodness is preserved and they naturally do not indulge in dregs and lees. You who are sons should listen attentively to the constant instructions of your fathers; you must not regard caution with wine as a minor virtue, for whether a virtue is great or small, you should view it as one and the same. You who are grandsons should listen clearly to the invariable instructions of your grandfathers; you must not regard caution with wine as a minor goodness, for whether a goodness is great or small, you should view it without distinction." Such was King Wen's teaching on being cautious with wine. Now, how can you people of the land of Mei not know to be cautious? You must carry on the strength of your limbs without sloth, and exhaust the toil of your callused hands and feet…

兄可也肇牽車牛遠事商賈致孝以養其父母
可也夫既務農以盡孝敬則父母之心懽然於

translation_en:
…without neglect or idleness. You may broadly cultivate millet and grain, toiling in the fields and hastening about to serve your fathers and elder brothers; or you may set out leading your ox-carts, engaging in distant commerce and trade, fulfilling filial devotion to nourish your parents. Once one devotes oneself to agriculture so as to fulfill filial reverence, the hearts of one's parents will delight in a world of wearing silk and eating meat; once one engages in trade so as to fulfill filial care, the hearts of one's parents will rejoice in a realm of full bellies and warm clothing. Then at such times, even if one washes the vessels to achieve purity and pours from that large goblet, it does no harm; even if one prepares rich fare to show generosity and pours from that rhinoceros-horn cup, it is no excess. Ah! Such was King Wu's teaching on the use of wine—how thorough was that with which he instructed Kangshu! Alas, the Announcement about Drunkenness (Jiugao) was originally composed to prohibit the people of Yin from indulging in wine. Yet in the text it says, first, that when parents rejoice one may drink wine; second, that when one is able to present offerings to the aged one may drink wine; and again, that when presenting sacrificial food one may drink wine. Originally intending to prohibit and put an end to their drinking, he instead opened up occasions for it—this is what is called a prohibition that does not prohibit. Such is the way the teaching of the sages does not coerce, and yet the people follow!

Classic of Poetry (Shijing):
"Heavy lies the dew, not dried save by the sun. Peaceful is the night drinking; without getting drunk, there is no returning. Heavy lies the dew, upon that luxuriant grass. Peaceful is the night drinking; in the ancestral chamber it is brought to completion."

Lu Yuanzhi 陸淵之

同考試官編修吳批此作不拘拘於繩墨但意
到即落筆故自有佳處他卷罕及之
同考試官編修張批七篇皆詞老氣壯非拘拘
於舉子業者此篇深得盛世君臣相與之意錄之
考試官學士萬批健筆寫出先王禮遇臣下之
情可愛可愛
考試官學士劉批君臣合故治道美可謂有見
者也
===
詩人既興君之燕臣也其情厚復興君之燕臣
也其情親盖君臣之間不可以分疎也有周人
君之燕臣既厚而且親焉其待遇之禮不既隆
哉此天子燕諸侯之詩想其燕飲之終歌之若
曰湛湛露斯天之澤也天澤之厚如此匪陽則
不晞焉君之燕臣也籩豆有楚殽核維旅主
而為明君賓而為賢臣歡然相接千載一遇是
以厭厭夜飲不醉則無帰焉曰厭厭夜飲者不
以久而懈其情曰不醉無帰者不以嚴而不盡

詩人既興君之燕臣也，其情厚；復興君之燕臣也，其情親。盖君臣之間，不可以分疎也。有周人君之燕臣，既厚而且親焉，其待遇之禮，不既隆哉！此天子燕諸侯之詩，想其燕飲之終，歌之若曰：「湛湛露斯」，天之澤也，天澤之厚如此，「匪陽」則「不晞」焉。君之燕臣也，籩豆有楚，殽核維旅，主而為明君，賓而為賢臣，歡然相接，千載一遇，是以「厭厭夜飲，不醉」則「無帰」焉。曰「厭厭夜飲」者，不以久而懈其情；曰「不醉無帰」者，不以嚴而不盡
translation_en:
… Yet this essay is grand in scope and radiant in spirit, and its conclusion carries weight where it belongs; it is a fine piece of work.
Associate Examiner Compiler Wu comments: This piece is not rigidly bound by conventional rules, yet wherever the thought reaches, the brush follows, so it naturally has its own merits that other papers rarely match.
Associate Examiner Compiler Zhang comments: All seven essays are mature in diction and vigorous in spirit, not rigidly bound to standard examination writing. This piece deeply grasps the spirit of mutual fellowship between ruler and minister in a flourishing age; let it be recorded for publication.
Examiner Academician Wan comments: With a vigorous brush, he has captured the sentiments with which the former kings treated their subordinates with courtesy—delightful, truly delightful!
Examiner Academician Liu comments: When ruler and minister are in harmony, the way of governance is admirable; this may be called the work of a man of insight.

The poet first uses an evocative image to show that in the ruler's feasting of his ministers, his feelings are generous; he then uses another evocative image to show that in the ruler's feasting of his ministers, his feelings are intimate. For between ruler and minister, there must not be estrangement on account of status. When the rulers of the Zhou feasted their ministers with both generosity and intimacy, was not the ritual of their treatment grand indeed! This is an ode for the Son of Heaven feasting the feudal lords. One may imagine that at the close of the banquet, they sang it as if to say: "Heavy lies the dew"—this is the grace of Heaven; so generous is Heaven's grace that "without the sun it does not dry." When the ruler feasts his ministers, the bamboo and wooden vessels are arrayed in neat order, and the meats and fruits are set forth in rows. The host is an enlightened ruler, and the guests are worthy ministers; joyously they meet, an encounter of a thousand years. Therefore, "happily we drink at night, and do not return home before we are drunk." Saying "happily we drink at night" means that they do not let their feelings slacken on account of the length of time; saying "we do not return home before we are drunk" means that they do not fail to express to the full…

同考試官郎中何　批〔此承上章王之藎臣無念爾祖而言而朱傳亦以此章言周之子孫臣庶當以文王爲法作者多昧本旨惟此篇體貼明白〕〔詞語諄切足以感動人心深得周公進戒之意必嘗究心〕
punctuated:
其情也。君之燕臣，何厚哉！詩人言之不足，又歌之，若曰：「湛湛露斯」，天之澤也，天澤之厚如此，則「在豐草」焉；君之燕臣也，兕觥其觼，旨酒思柔，君而為賢主，臣而為嘉賓，怡然相契，萬古一逢，是以「厭厭夜飲，在宗」而「載考」焉。曰「在宗」，所以示親之之意；曰「載考」，則亦未嘗忘其禮也。君之燕臣，何親哉！吁！天澤厚而下被，君恩厚而下及，詩人褒揚歌詠之意美矣。雖然，君之燕臣，事之常者耳，聖人何錄之經耶？誠以君臣會合，治道所繫。周惟君臣合，故治道美而後世莫及；秦惟以□自尊，使君臣之分不啻霄壤，遂一傳而失其祚。然則聖人垂示之意深矣。

「無念爾祖，聿修厥德。永言配命，自求多福。」
林孟和
同考試官郎中何批：此承上章「王之藎臣，無念爾祖」而言，而《朱傳》亦以此章言周之子孫臣庶當以文王為法，作者多昧本旨。惟此篇體貼明白，詞語諄切，足以感動人心，深得周公進戒之意，必嘗究心
translation_en:
…their feelings. When the ruler feasts his ministers, how generous he is!

When the poet found mere words insufficient, he sang of it again, as if to say: "Heavy lies the dew"—that is the grace of Heaven; when Heaven's grace is as generous as this, it rests "upon the luxuriant grass." When the ruler feasts his ministers, the rhinoceros-horn goblets are curved and the fine wine is mellow; the ruler acts as a worthy host and the ministers as honored guests, delighting in mutual accord in an encounter rare in ten thousand ages. Therefore, "happily they drink at night, in the ancestral temple chamber," and so "complete the feast." Saying "in the ancestral temple chamber" is the way to display the intention of treating them with intimacy; saying "complete the feast" shows that they nonetheless never forgot the proper rites. When the ruler feasts his ministers, how intimate he is!

Ah! Heaven's grace is generous and reaches down below; the ruler's favor is generous and extends to his subordinates. Admirable indeed is the intent of the poet's praise and song! Even so, a ruler feasting his ministers is merely an ordinary affair—why did the Sage record it in the Classic? Truly it is because the harmonious union of ruler and minister is that upon which the Way of governance depends. Only because ruler and minister were united in the Zhou was its Way of governance admirable and unsurpassed by later ages; only because the Qin exalted itself through [?], making the gulf between ruler and minister no less than that between heaven and earth, did it lose its throne after a single generation. Thus the intention of the Sage in handing down this lesson is profound indeed.

"Ever think of your ancestor, and cultivate your virtue. Forever conform to the Mandate, and seek for yourselves much blessing."
Lin Menghe

Comment by Associate Examiner Director He: This passage continues the thought of the preceding stanza, "The King's loyal ministers, ever think of your ancestor," and Zhu Xi's Commentary (Zhu zhuan) likewise takes this stanza as saying that the descendants, ministers, and common people of Zhou ought to take King Wen as their model. Most writers are blind to the original purport. This essay alone closely and clearly grasps the text; its language is earnest and moving enough to stir people's hearts, deeply capturing the Duke of Zhou's intent in offering admonition. He must be one who has devoted his mind…

title: 成化二年會試錄

於見聞者
同考試官編修呉批此是守規矩文字意思
縝密無可破綻使推此以見之行事亦孰得而議之
同考試官編修張批此篇一以敬立説得周公
進戒之意且行文謹密非騁浮詞者故録之

考試官學士劉批末引孟子之言以斷商周之
事尤高
大臣之勉君臣惟皆盡法祖之事斯得法祖之應
===
盖法祖圖治君臣所當務也誠能修徳循理而
盡法祖之事則多福之應豈待外求而得哉是
詩周公戒成王而作此言周之子孫臣庶當以
文王為法意謂商之孫子侯于周服爾祖文王
緝熙敬止之徳所致也爾周之子孫觀彼侯服
之在周獨無感于中而念爾祖之徳乎殷士膚
敏祼將于京亦爾祖文王緝熙敬止之徳所致
也爾周之臣庶覩彼□□之在廟寧不動于心
而念爾祖之徳乎然所以念之惟在修徳循理而

於見聞者。
同考試官編修呉批：此是守規矩文字，意思縝密，無可破綻。使推此以見之行事，亦孰得而議之？

考試官學士劉批：末引孟子之言，以斷商周之事，尤高。
大臣之勉君臣，惟皆盡法祖之事，斯得法祖之應。盖法祖圖治，君臣所當務也。誠能修徳循理，而盡法祖之事，則多福之應，豈待外求而得哉？是詩周公戒成王而作，此言周之子孫臣庶，當以文王為法。意謂商之孫子，侯于周服，爾祖文王緝熙敬止之徳所致也。爾周之子孫，觀彼侯服之在周，獨無感于中而念爾祖之徳乎？殷士膚敏，祼將于京，亦爾祖文王緝熙敬止之徳所致也。爾周之臣庶，覩彼□□之在廟，寧不動于心而念爾祖之徳乎？然所以念之，惟在修徳循理而…
translation_en:
… what he has seen and heard.
Comment by Associate Examiner Compiler Wu: This is an essay that adheres strictly to the rules; its reasoning is meticulous and without flaw. If one were to extend this and manifest it in practical conduct, who could possibly find fault with it?
Comment by Associate Examiner Compiler Zhang: This piece establishes its argument entirely upon reverence, capturing the Duke of Zhou's intent in offering admonition. Moreover, its composition is careful and tight, not one that indulges in empty rhetoric; therefore it is selected for inclusion.
Comment by Examiner Academician Wan: Both the diction and the meaning are fully realized, deeply according with the fundamental purport of the text.
Comment by Examiner Academician Liu: At the end, his quoting the words of Mencius to judge the affairs of Shang and Zhou is especially lofty.
When a great minister exhorts both sovereign and subjects, it is only when all fulfill the task of modeling themselves on their ancestor that they obtain the response of modeling themselves on their ancestor. For modeling oneself on the ancestors and planning for good governance are what both sovereign and subjects ought to devote themselves to. If they can truly cultivate virtue and follow principle, thereby fulfilling the task of modeling themselves on their ancestor, then how would the response of abundant blessings require seeking from the outside in order to be obtained? This ode was composed by the Duke of Zhou to admonish King Cheng, and this stanza states that the descendants, officials, and commoners of Zhou ought to take King Wen as their model. The meaning is that the descendants of Shang became lords subject to Zhou because of the virtue of your ancestor King Wen in maintaining continuous and bright reverence. When you, the descendants of Zhou, observe those subject lords present in Zhou, how could you alone feel nothing within and fail to be mindful of your ancestor's virtue? That the officers of Yin, fine and agile, assist at the libation sacrifices in the capital is likewise brought about by the virtue of your ancestor King Wen in maintaining continuous and bright reverence. When you, the officials and commoners of Zhou, behold those [libation-assistants?] present in the ancestral temple, how could you not be moved in your hearts to be mindful of your ancestor's virtue? Yet the way to be mindful of him lies solely in cultivating virtue and following principle, and…

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
已也為子孫者當以爾祖敬德為法而自勉又
常加自省使無一事不合天理可也為臣庶者
當以爾祖敬德是式而自修又常加自察俾無
一行不循天道可也若然則保其家邦多歷年
所而簡簡之福萃於子孫者有不外求而得矣
保其祿位與國咸休而穰穰之福集於臣庶者
又豈他求而至哉周公以是為言盖以周之臣
庶既當法乎文王則為子孫者尤當法乎文王
也其戒成王之意不既深歟抑此以前一則言
===
命周之福不惟及其子孫而又及其群臣之後
嗣也一則言絕商之禍不惟及其子孫而又及
其群臣之後嗣也吁周有大德天故福之商惟
滅德天故禍之是商自求禍周自求福耳天何
容心於其間哉孟子曰禍福無不自己求之者
其商周之謂歟
侯主侯伯侯亞侯旅侯彊侯以有嗿其饁
思媚其婦有依其士有略其耜俶載南畝
播厥百穀實函斯活驛驛其達有厭其傑

又豈他求而至哉周公以是爲言蓋以周之臣
庶旣當法乎文王則爲子孫者尤當法乎文王
也其戒成王之意不旣深歟抑此以前一則言
===
命周之福不惟及其子孫而又及其群臣之後
嗣也一則言絕商之禍不惟及其子孫而又及
其群臣之後嗣也吁周有大德天故福之商惟
滅德天故禍之是商自求禍周自求福耳天何
容心於其間哉孟子曰禍福無不自己求之者
其商周之謂歟
侯主侯伯侯亞侯旅侯彊侯以有嗿其饁
思媚其婦有依其士有略其耜俶載南畝
播厥百穀實函斯活驛驛其達有厭其傑
punctuated:
已也。為子孫者，當以爾祖敬德為法而自勉，又常加自省，使無一事不合天理可也；為臣庶者，當以爾祖敬德是式而自修，又常加自察，俾無一行不循天道可也。若然，則保其家邦，多歷年所，而簡簡之福萃於子孫者，有不外求而得矣；保其祿位，與國咸休，而穰穰之福集於臣庶者，又豈他求而至哉？周公以是為言，盖以周之臣庶既當法乎文王，則為子孫者尤當法乎文王也。其戒成王之意，不既深歟？抑此以前，一則言命周之福，不惟及其子孫，而又及其群臣之後嗣也；一則言絕商之禍，不惟及其子孫，而又及其群臣之後嗣也。吁！周有大德，天故福之；商惟滅德，天故禍之。是商自求禍，周自求福耳，天何容心於其間哉？孟子曰：「禍福無不自己求之者。」其商、周之謂歟？

侯主侯伯，侯亞侯旅，侯彊侯以。有嗿其饁，思媚其婦，有依其士。有略其耜，俶載南畝，播厥百穀，實函斯活，驛驛其達，有厭其傑，
translation_en:
…[in cultivating virtue and following principle] alone. Those who are descendants ought to take the reverent virtue of your ancestor as their model and exert themselves, and also constantly examine themselves so that not a single affair fails to accord with Heavenly Principle. Those who are ministers and subjects ought to take the reverent virtue of your ancestor as their pattern and cultivate themselves, and also constantly scrutinize themselves so that not a single action fails to follow the Way of Heaven. If this is done, then in preserving their ruling house and state through the passage of many years, abundant blessings will gather upon the descendants, obtained without seeking them from outside; and in preserving their emoluments and positions to share in the state's prosperity, plentiful blessings will collect upon the ministers and subjects—how could these be brought about by seeking them elsewhere? The Duke of Zhou spoke in this way because, since the ministers and subjects of Zhou ought to model themselves on King Wen, those who are his descendants ought all the more to model themselves on King Wen. Is not the intent of his admonition to King Cheng profound indeed? Furthermore, prior to this passage, on the one hand the poem speaks of how the blessings of the Mandate conferred on Zhou extended not only to its descendants, but also to the posterity of its many ministers; on the other hand, it speaks of how the calamity of cutting off Shang extended not only to its descendants, but also to the posterity of its many ministers. Alas! Zhou possessed great virtue, and therefore Heaven blessed it; Shang destroyed its virtue, and therefore Heaven brought calamity upon it. This means that Shang sought calamity for itself and Zhou sought blessings for itself—how could Heaven harbor any deliberate partiality between them? Mencius said: "Calamity and blessing are in every case sought by oneself." Does this not refer to Shang and Zhou?

"There are the master and the eldest son, the younger brothers and the multitude of kinsmen, the helpers of surplus strength and the hired laborers. Loud is the sound of their eating the food brought to the fields; loving are their wives, and comforted are their husbands. Sharp are their plowshares, as they begin work on the southern acres. They sow all the kinds of grain, the seeds holding a living germ; thick and fast the shoots spring up; well-nourished are the tallest blades,…"

translation_en:
…even and regular grows the young grain, and closely, carefully runs the weeding. Then come the reapers in crowds, and the grain is piled up solidly in the fields, in tens of thousands, millions, and hundreds of millions. It is made into spirits and sweet must, to offer to our ancestors and ancestresses, and so to fulfill all the hundred rites.

Lu Yuanzhi 陸淵之

Comment by Associate Examiner and Director (langzhong) He: Most who wrote on this topic remained narrowly bogged down in agricultural details, which was quite unsatisfactory. Only this composition depicts the atmosphere of great peace under the Zhou dynasty so vividly that it seems right before one's eyes—truly not a rigid or pedantic way of interpreting the Odes!

Comment by Associate Examiner and Historiography Compiler (bianxiu) Wu: Everyone in the examination hall was able to write on this topic, but when they reached the passage "noisily they eat the food brought to the fields" [written here as 有饛其饁], their phrasing became awkward and superfluous, failing to form proper parallel couplets. This composition alone is nimble and lively, completely unconstrained, and moreover captures the spirit of village folk and rustic elders working hard at farming in those days. It is truly a fine piece.

Comment by Associate Examiner and Historiography Compiler (bianxiu) Zhang: The Sacrificial Odes (Song) are fundamentally meant to praise and give form to flourishing virtue. That this essay brings out the atmosphere of a well-governed age is admirable, and its wording is furthermore free of petty trivialities. He must be a fine scholar.

Comment by Examiner and Academician (xueshi) Wan: The passage set as the topic is inherently long, yet he is able to condense it while fully recounting the Zhou people's farming, harvesting, and sacrificial rites, standing far above the other compositions. Moreover, his three essays on the Analects (Lunyu), the Mencius (Mengzi), and the ode "Heavy Dew" (Zhanlu) have a mature and vigorous tone—how could immature works ever match them?

Comment by Examiner and Academician (xueshi) Liu: The atmosphere of great peace among the people of Zhou can be seen in this essay.

When human effort is exerted to the utmost, the young grain grows luxuriantly; when the harvest is abundant, the sacrificial rites are carried out in full. From this, one may behold the atmosphere of great peace under the Zhou dynasty. Now, agriculture was held in the highest regard by the ancients; the poet recounts in detail…

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
其始終而播諸歌頌太平氣象豈不見於言表
哉想夫有周盛時人皆務農當夫東作方興衆
力競勸內而主伯亞旅之咸集外而侯彊侯以
之皆在斯時也食其饁餉嗿然有聲夫媚其婦
視耕作為何勞婦依其夫以饁餉為當務有略
其耜而備之也豫俶載南畝而耕之也勤由是
百穀以播含氣而漸生也苗生出土氣足而先
長也苗既厭厭而茂盛矣耘復緜緜而詳密焉
迨夫平秩西成銍艾攸舉穫之桎桎者濟濟其
===

translation_en: …them from beginning to end and broadcast them in songs and hymns—how could the atmosphere of great peace not be visible beyond the words themselves? Imagine the flourishing age of the Zhou, when everyone devoted themselves to agriculture. Just when the spring fieldwork was beginning and the strength of the multitude competed in mutual encouragement, inside the family the master, the eldest son, the younger sons, and the younger kin all gathered together, while from outside the strong helpers and the hired hands were all present. At this time, as they ate the food brought to the fields, there was a cheerful sound of dining; husbands cherished their wives, regarding the toil of plowing as no hardship at all, while wives relied on their husbands, taking the delivery of meals to the fields as their proper duty. Sharp were their plowshares, prepared beforehand; they began their work on the southern acres, plowing with diligence. From this, the hundred grains were sown, holding vital energy within and gradually sprouting; the shoots emerged from the soil, their vital energy abundant, growing up ahead of the weeds. Once the shoots were glossy and luxuriant, the weeding in turn proceeded in unbroken lines, thorough and meticulous. By the time the autumn harvest was regulated and completed, and the short sickles were put to work, those reaping with a ringing sound were numerous and stately in their multitude; that which was stacked in solid, dense piles numbered in the tens of thousands, hundreds of millions, and billions. From this, when fermented into wine, there was the clearness and coolness of the Three Wines; when brewed into sweet spirits, there was the fragrant aroma of the Five Sacrificial Liquors. Thereupon these were presented to the ancestors and ancestresses, and thereupon the sincerity of filial offerings was fully expressed. The sacrifices encompass a hundred rites, and here they were brought into complete harmony; ritual propriety embodies ten moral relationships, and here they were made all-encompassing. Ah! Human effort was exerted to the utmost during the season of plowing and weeding, and the sacrificial rites were prepared in full at the time of an abundant harvest—such indeed was the atmosphere of great peace under the Zhou! Even so, the atmosphere of great peace is not seen merely in devotion to agricultural tasks and the preparation of sacrificial rites alone. The following lines of the ode say: "Richly fragrant is the aroma, the glory of the state and the family; pervasive is the scent of pepper, bringing peace to the aged and long-lived." Viewing the whole together, one can see in it the thickness of moral human relationships, one can see in it the purity of customs and moral transformation, and one can see in it the rise of harmony and joy…

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
考試官學士劉批〔春秋之初人知有王而無伯春秋之末人知有伯而無王孔子懼而作春秋此類是也此篇得之〕
伯啓於內諸侯從而復貳伯竊於外諸侯從而
即違于此見禮義之天猶未泯於春秋之人心
也既夫姬轍不西乾綱失馭天下日趨於伯矣
齊桓假平宋之名倡北杏之會大國如宋陳既
協相其猷小邦如蔡邾亦奔走其事夫齊桓一
會而四國從之罔敢差池吾方責諸侯之始亂
===
也孰知其猶不甘心於齊耶已而北杏之壇坫
方掃諸侯之叛心漸興微子之宋首以背會而
蒙伐叔度之蔡尋以懷貳而受侵神明之陳又
以避軍之釁而來濤塗之執焉是何三國忘齊
之速哉蓋亦念夫周德雖衰天命未改桓非受
命之伯而我從之有弗忍耳是非尊王黜伯之
天猶未泯與若夫文襄既遠晉伯日微世道又
將胥淪於夷矣楚虔號召中華之國大講于申
之會若宋若鄭皆獻禮而薦聞若邾若滕悉拱

伯啓於內，諸侯從而復貳；伯竊於外，諸侯從而即違。于此見禮義之天猶未泯於春秋之人心也。既夫姬轍不西，乾綱失馭，天下日趨於伯矣。齊桓假平宋之名，倡北杏之會，大國如宋、陳，既協相其猷；小邦如蔡、邾，亦奔走其事。夫齊桓一會而四國從之，罔敢差池，吾方責諸侯之始亂也，孰知其猶不甘心於齊耶？已而北杏之壇坫方掃，諸侯之叛心漸興。微子之宋，首以背會而蒙伐；叔度之蔡，尋以懷貳而受侵；神明之陳，又以避軍之釁而來濤塗之執焉。是何三國忘齊之速哉？蓋亦念夫周德雖衰，天命未改，桓非受命之伯，而我從之，有弗忍耳。是非尊王黜伯之天猶未泯與？若夫文、襄既遠，晉伯日微，世道又將胥淪於夷矣。楚虔號召中華之國，大講于申之會。若宋若鄭，皆獻禮而薦聞；若邾若滕，悉拱

Examiner and Academician Liu comments: 〔At the beginning of the Spring and Autumn period, people knew there was the King and no hegemon; at the end of the Spring and Autumn period, people knew there were hegemons and no King. Confucius was afraid and composed the Spring and Autumn Annals—matters of this sort are what it was about. This essay has grasped it.〕

When hegemony was initiated within the central states, the feudal lords followed and yet turned disloyal again; when hegemony was usurped from the outside, the feudal lords followed and yet immediately defied it. From this we see that the heavenly principle of propriety and righteousness had still not been extinguished in the minds of the people of the Spring and Autumn period. Once the carriage tracks of the Ji royal house of Zhou no longer went west and the sovereign authority lost its control, the world daily hastened toward霸 (hegemony). Duke Huan of Qi (Qi Huan 齊桓), borrowing the name of pacifying Song, initiated the covenant meeting at Beixing. Great states like Song and Chen assisted in his plans, while small states like Cai and Zhu also scurried to serve his cause. Now, when Duke Huan of Qi held a single meeting and four states followed him without daring to falter, I was just reproaching the feudal lords for beginning the disorder—who would have known that they were still not content in their hearts to submit to Qi? Before long, when the altar and mound at Beixing had barely been swept clear, rebellious thoughts among the feudal lords gradually arose. Song, the state of Weizi, was the first to suffer punitive attack for turning its back on the meeting; Cai, the state of Shudu, soon suffered invasion for harboring duplicity; and Chen, descendant of the divine sage Shun, because of the rift over diverting the army's march, brought about the seizure of Yuan Taotu (濤塗). Why were these three states so quick to forget Qi? Surely it was because they reflected that although the virtue of Zhou had declined, the Mandate of Heaven had not changed; Huan was not a hegemon who had received the royal mandate, and in following him, there was something they could not bear to do. Is this not proof that the heavenly principle of honoring the King and rejecting the hegemon had still not been extinguished? As for the time when Dukes Wen and Xiang were already distant in the past and the hegemony of Jin grew daily weaker, the way of the world was about to sink altogether into that of the barbarians. Qian of Chu (Chu Qian 楚虔, King Ling of Chu) summoned the states of the central lands and held a grand assembly at the covenant meeting of Shen. 手以聽命。夫楚虔一呼，而諸國應之，惟恐或後。吾方憫人心之陷溺也，孰意其能不終事於楚耶？已而于申罷會，伐吳有役，獻禮之左師，賦一跡之不臨；舊守之子產，亦一介之不與；以至鄒、滕之君，亦望望然去之，而不同其事焉。是何諸國去楚之亟哉？蓋亦念夫晉伯雖微，主盟猶舊；彼荆蠻，大邦之讎，而我從之，有足羞耳。是則貴華賤夷之天，猶未泯與！吁！即諸侯背齊，而知人心之有周，有王者作，則文、武之業可興；即諸侯棄楚，而知人心之有晉，有伯者作，則文、襄之盛可復。惜乎周不復興，而世道為齊、晉；晉不復興，而世道為吳、楚、於越矣。重可慨也夫！

晉侯及楚子、鄭伯戰于鄢陵，楚子、鄭師敗績〔成公十六年〕。晉韓厥帥師伐鄭，仲孫蔑會齊崔杼、曹人、邾人、杞人次于鄫〔襄公元年〕。會于戚、蕭魚〔襄公十一年〕。楚公子午帥師伐鄭〔襄公十八年〕。楚子、蔡侯、陳侯、許男伐鄭〔襄公二十四年〕。楚子、蔡侯、陳侯伐鄭〔襄公二十六年〕。
translation_en:
…folded their hands to obey his commands. When Chu Qian (King Ling of Chu) gave a single shout, the various states responded, fearing only that they might be left behind. Just as I was lamenting how deeply human hearts had sunk, who would have thought that they could refrain from serving Chu to the end? Before long, after the covenant at Shen concluded and the campaign against Wu was launched, the Master of the Left (Xiang Xu of Song), who had previously presented ceremonial protocols, did not set a single foot [in the campaign] to contribute military levies [?]; Zichan (of Zheng), who had held to old precedents, likewise did not send a single envoy to participate; and even the rulers of Zou (Zhu) and Teng walked away in high dudgeon and refused to share in the enterprise. Why were the various states so quick to abandon Chu? It was surely because they reflected that although the hegemony of Jin had weakened, it was still the longstanding leader of the covenants; whereas those Jing barbarians (Chu) were the enemies of the great central states, and to follow them was truly shameful! Does this not show that the heavenly principle of prizing the Chinese and despising the barbarians had not yet perished?

Alas! From the fact that the feudal lords turned their backs on Qi, we know that the House of Zhou still remained in people's hearts; had a true king arisen, the enterprise of Kings Wen and Wu could have been revived. From the fact that the feudal lords abandoned Chu, we know that Jin still remained in people's hearts; had a true hegemon arisen, the flourishing of Dukes Wen and Xiang could have been restored. How regrettable that Zhou did not revive, and the way of the world fell to Qi and Jin; and when Jin did not revive, the way of the world fell to Wu, Chu, and Yuyue (Yue)! It is deeply lamentable indeed!

The Marquis of Jin fought with the Viscount of Chu and the Earl of Zheng at Yanling; the Viscount of Chu and the army of Zheng suffered a crushing defeat [16th year of Duke Cheng]. Han Jue of Jin led an army to attack Zheng; Zhongsun Mie met with Cui Zhu of Qi, and men of Cao, Zhu, and Qi, and halted at Zeng [1st year of Duke Xiang]. [The lords] met at Qi and at Xiaoyu [11th year of Duke Xiang]. Prince Wu of Chu led an army to attack Zheng [18th year of Duke Xiang]. The Viscount of Chu, the Marquis of Cai, the Marquis of Chen, and the Baron of Xu attacked Zheng [24th year of Duke Xiang]. The Viscount of Chu, the Marquis of Cai, and the Marquis of Chen attacked Zheng [26th year of Duke Xiang].

同考試官主事左批説鄭從晋從楚之得失
有關鍵其視騁浮詞畧事實者異目語也
同考試官編修汪批題本傳意而場中作者
膠於鄢陵幸勝之説殊戾其旨此篇體認親切
而文足以發之是用錄出
考試官學士萬批體認鄭從楚從晋得失甚
親切
考試官學士劉批鄭介乎夷夏之間而難於
===
立國如此聖人所以嘆周之衰而不能綱紀四方也此篇
其知經之意矣乎
貳國從夷而懷其惠故伯主服之也難從伯而
感其誠故外夷爭之也難此鄭人不忘晋楚雖
同而事有得失之異也且汝陰之田既成而鄭
與楚之心固矣乃今鄢陵之役晋厲因討鄭而
興師楚子欲庇鄭而来救而鄭也左右乎楚遂
相與戮力以禦晋焉當是之時晋雖收一矢之
捷而無以挽鄭之北從楚雖遭中目之傷而益

Comment by Associate Examiner and Secretary Zuo: Its discussion of the gains and losses in Zheng's following Jin versus following Chu hits the key point; compared to those who indulge in empty rhetoric and gloss over historical facts, this speaks on a wholly different level.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Historiographer Wang: The question is based on the meaning of the commentary, yet writers in the examination hall clung to the theory of a fortunate victory at Yanling, which goes quite against its purport. This essay grasps the point intimately, and the writing suffices to bring it out; therefore it is selected for inclusion.
Comment by Examiner and Academician Wan: It grasps the gains and losses of Zheng's following Chu versus following Jin most intimately.
Comment by Examiner and Academician Liu: That Zheng was caught between the barbarians and the Chinese States, making it so difficult to establish the state, is why the Sage sighed over the decline of Zhou and its inability to bring order to the four quarters. Does not this essay understand the meaning of the Classic!
When a wavering state follows the barbarians and cherishes their favors, it is difficult for a hegemon to win its submission; when it follows the hegemon and is moved by his sincerity, it is difficult for foreign barbarians to contend for it. Thus, although the people of Zheng were alike in not forgetting Jin and Chu, in practice there was a difference between gain and loss. Moreover, once the lands of Ruyin had been granted in peace, Zheng's heart in allying with Chu was firm. Then, in the campaign of Yanling, Duke Li of Jin raised an army to punish Zheng, the Viscount of Chu came to the rescue out of a desire to shelter Zheng, and Zheng assisted Chu on the left and right, joining forces to resist Jin. At that time, although Jin reaped the victory of a single arrow, it had no way to draw Zheng into following the north; and although Chu suffered a wound that struck the eye, it all the more…

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
以堅鄭之南向鄭於斯時殆楚之縣鄙爾未幾
二載悼公復伯風采一新吾意鄭人不勞兵甲
而自來矣奈何生死從夷志猶前日悼公於是
首伐以韓厥之師重威以列卿之次伐則伐矣
而請成之使不聞次則次矣而息肩之意何有
晉何其服鄭之難耶假曰楚惠在鄭未忍忘也
然棄中國從蠻夷而不以大義裁之曾得為善
乎自是厥後悼公務求善勝之道鄭人頓改南
向之轅蕭魚有會伯騈行成遂相與同心以講
===
好焉當是之時晉以誠感而無鄭虞鄭以誠服
而無晉詐則今日之鄭非鄢陵之鄭矣曽幾何
年悼公不祿楚復爭鄭吾恐其一鼓而鄭可下
也惟其從晉之心始終不貳楚也一伐不已而
棘澤之師繼至再伐無何而南里之入踵來忿
非不逞也而無以間其內從威非不黷也而不
能脅其外附楚何其爭鄭之難耶雖曰晉德在
鄭不可忘也然貴中國賤夷狄而不怵威之屈
豈非賢乎吁人知晉服鄭之難而不知亦厲公
