punctuated: 以堅鄭之南向。鄭於斯時，殆楚之縣鄙爾。未幾二載，悼公復伯，風采一新，吾意鄭人不勞兵甲而自來矣。奈何生死從夷，志猶前日。悼公於是首伐以韓厥之師，重威以列卿之次。伐則伐矣，而請成之使不聞；次則次矣，而息肩之意何有？晉何其服鄭之難耶！假曰楚惠在鄭，未忍忘也，然棄中國、從蠻夷，而不以大義裁之，曾得為善乎？自是厥後，悼公務求善勝之道，鄭人頓改南向之轅，蕭魚有會，伯騈行成，遂相與同心以講好焉。當是之時，晉以誠感而無鄭虞，鄭以誠服而無晉詐，則今日之鄭，非鄢陵之鄭矣。曽幾何年，悼公不祿，楚復爭鄭，吾恐其一鼓而鄭可下也。惟其從晉之心始終不貳，楚也一伐不已，而棘澤之師繼至；再伐無何，而南里之入踵來。忿非不逞也，而無以間其內從；威非不黷也，而不能脅其外附。楚何其爭鄭之難耶！雖曰晉德在鄭，不可忘也，然貴中國、賤夷狄，而不怵威之屈，豈非賢乎？吁！人知晉服鄭之難，而不知亦厲公
translation_en:
…further hardened Zheng's southward allegiance. At that time, Zheng was virtually a mere district or borderland of Chu. Scarcely two years later, Duke Dao (悼公) restored the hegemony, and his bearing and vigor were completely renewed; I would have thought the people of Zheng would come over of their own accord without the toil of weapons and armor. Yet how was it that, through life and death following the barbarians, their resolve remained as in former days? Duke Dao thereupon first attacked them with the army of Han Jue (韓厥), and reinforced his might by halting the ministers of the various states in camp. Attack they did, yet no envoy requesting peace was heard of; camp they did, yet what sign was there of any intention to rest their shoulders from the burden? How difficult it was for Jin to win the submission of Zheng! Even supposing one says that Chu's favor rested upon Zheng and they could not bear to forget it, yet to abandon the Central States and follow the southern barbarians without judging the matter by great righteousness—how could that be considered good?

Thereafter, Duke Dao devoted himself to seeking the way of winning well, and the people of Zheng suddenly turned around their southward-bound chariots. There was the covenant at Xiaoyu (蕭魚), and Bo Pian (伯騈) went to conclude peace, whereupon they joined in single-minded harmony to cultivate friendly relations. At that time, Jin moved them with sincerity and had no anxiety over Zheng, while Zheng submitted out of sincerity and harbored no deceit toward Jin; thus the Zheng of this day was no longer the Zheng of Yanling (鄢陵). How many years had passed before Duke Dao died, and Chu once again contended for Zheng? I would have feared that at the first drumbeat Zheng could be brought down. Only because its heart in following Jin remained undivided from beginning to end, Chu attacked once without ceasing, and the army at Jize (棘澤) followed closely after; it attacked a second time, and before long the incursion into Nanli (南里) came on its heels. Its wrath was not unvented, yet it had no means to drive a wedge in Zheng's internal allegiance; its might was not unspent, yet it could not coerce Zheng into external attachment. How difficult it was for Chu to contend for Zheng! Even though one says that Jin's virtue rested upon Zheng and could not be forgotten, yet to honor the Central States, despise the barbarians, and not be cowed into submission by intimidation—was this not worthy? Alas! People know how difficult it was for Jin to win the submission of Zheng, yet they do not know that it was also because Duke Li's (厲公)…

translation_en:
…strength reached others only shallowly; they know how difficult it was for Chu to contend for Zheng, yet do not know that it was because Duke Dao's sincerity entered into people's hearts so deeply. Viewed from this perspective, one can see that subjugating others by force is ultimately not as good as winning their submission through virtue. Alas! "He who soothes us is our sovereign; he who oppresses us is our enemy"—human hearts and heavenly principle are the same across ten thousand ages as in a single day. Who could say that Zheng of the Spring and Autumn period could be bullied through power and force!

"The Duke and the Marquis of Qi sought to make peace between Ju and Tan, but the people of Ju were unwilling" [fourth year of Duke Xuan]; "The Duke met the Marquis of Qi at Jiagu" [tenth year of Duke Ding].

By Zhong Fan 鍾蕃.

Comment by Associate Examiner and Secretary Zuo 左: [The topic itself is plain and straightforward, and writers can generally speak to it, yet none have shown brushwork as concise and vigorous without departing from the purport of the topic as this essay does.]
Comment by Associate Examiner and Historiographer Wang 汪: [Where this essay elucidates Duke Xuan of Lu pursuing private ends in trying to pacify Ju, and Confucius reproving Qi through ritual propriety, the diction is upright and rigorous—something immature compositions cannot attain.]
Comment by Examiner and Academician Wan 萬: [The traces of trying to pacify Ju and transforming Qi naturally manifest themselves in the phrasing.]
Comment by Examiner and Academician Liu 劉: [When a sage is employed even on a small scale, the result is already like this; how much more so if he were employed on a grand scale? What this essay elucidates makes that evident.]

When one coerces others through power, the great cannot enforce their will even upon the small [reading 大 for 人]; when one reproves others through ritual propriety, the weak can win the submission of the strong. The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) fully records our state of Lu's affairs in trying to pacify Ju and in meeting with Qi, so as to show that power is insufficient to rely upon whereas ritual propriety can be relied upon. Why is this? Tan and Ju had accumulated grievances and refused to yield to one another…

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
久矣今也魯宣君國與郯有連為之平莒□
齊以為重焉夫以千乘之大國而平蕞爾之小
邦使非在己弗公則不待文告之及而莒將聽
命之不暇矣奈何我公為人圖成內懷利欲而
弗能折衷以義外憑威力而無以取信於人故
莒雖小曾無忌憚而竟辭平焉盖彼之所以敢
於不從而我亦不能强其必從者要之以勢爾
徒以勢則大不能行之小何惑乎若夫齊魯交
兵而不相能甚矣今也夾谷之會齊景惑於犂
===
彌之言又將駕魯以逞志焉夫以積衰之魯而
當素强之齊使非得人與俱則鼓譟之兵遽起
而我君執辱之弗免矣幸而聖人攝行相事神

translation_en:
… for a long time. Now, when Duke Xuan of Lu ruled the state, because he had marriage ties with Tan, he sought to reconcile Ju on Tan's behalf, [and joined with?] Qi to add weight to the effort. Now, when major states of a thousand chariots seek to pacify a tiny statelet, had there not been a lack of impartiality in themselves, Ju would not even have waited for the diplomatic pronouncements to arrive before hastening to obey their commands. How could it be that our Duke, in trying to broker peace for another, internally harbored selfish desires for profit and could not adjudicate the matter with righteousness, while externally relying on coercive force and having no means to win the trust of others? Therefore, although Ju was small, it had not the slightest fear and in the end refused the reconciliation. Indeed, the reason they dared to disobey and we could not compel their obedience was that we coerced them merely through power. If one relies solely on power, then even the great cannot prevail over the small—what is there to be puzzled about?

As for Qi and Lu, they had engaged in armed conflict and been on extremely bad terms. Now, at the meeting at Jiagu, Duke Jing of Qi was misled by the words of Li Mi and once again intended to overpower Lu so as to gratify his ambitions. Facing the habitually strong Qi with the long-weakened Lu, had Lu not obtained the right man to accompany the ruler, clamoring troops would have suddenly risen up, and our ruler could not have escaped the humiliation of being seized. Fortunately, the Sage [Confucius] acted as chief minister of protocol: the swiftness of his marvelous transformative influence was able to put an end to their malicious plots, and his words of ritual propriety and righteousness were sufficient to correct their transgressions against ritual. Therefore, although Qi was strong, it had a change of heart and was only afraid of being too slow to feel shame and remorse. Indeed, the reason we were able to bring about their submission, and they could not help but submit, was that we reproved them with ritual propriety. If one acts through ritual propriety, then the weak can subdue the strong—what is there to wonder at [reading 惟 as 怪]?

Alas! For the great to oversee the small is natural and easy; why then could Qi and Lu not command Ju? For the weak to control the strong goes against the grain and is difficult; why then could Lu reform Qi? What is meant by the saying that in the world…

… under heaven nothing is greater than principle, and superior force and numbers have no part in it—there is truly good reason for this! Even so, after peace was arranged at [?]-jie [蜀階?], had Duke Ling (Linggong) been able to examine himself for the fault, the gentleman would still have judged his offense lightly; instead, he proceeded to attack them with troops and seize their towns in order to persist in his wrong—what could be more unrighteous than this? And after the meeting at Jiagu, had Duke Ding (Dinggong) been able to employ the Sage to the end, then not only would the encroached territories have been swiftly restored to their former state, but "transforming Qi until it reaches the level of Lu, and transforming Lu until it reaches the Way"—how would that have been merely consigned to empty words and nothing more? Alas!

"The Son of Heaven then offers a lamb and opens the ice, first presenting it in the rear apartments of the ancestral temple."
By Dong Lu 董輅.
Comment by Associate Examiner Historiographer Li 李: Most candidates writing on this topic do not understand the meaning of "offering a lamb." This essay uses concise and fitting diction without losing the principle; it ought to be placed among the selected ranks.
Comment by Associate Examiner Academician Reader-in-Waiting Liu 劉: The phrasing is smooth and the purport clear. Its elucidation of the meaning of "first presenting it in the rear apartments of the ancestral temple" is especially unmatched in other papers; he may truly be called an accomplished writer.
Comment by Examiner Academician Wan 萬: The passages on opening the ice and using the ice are explained thoroughly and clearly; worthy of selection.
Comment by Examiner Academician Liu 劉: In speaking of the filial heart of the gentleman toward his parents, it deeply grasps the fundamental purport.

Once the former kings had performed the rites to obtain a thing, they invariably used that thing to make an offering to their ancestors. Indeed, as for ice as a substance, the former kings' having uses for it goes back to antiquity. Yet they invariably performed the rites to sacrifice to the spirit before taking it out, and presented it in the temple out of reverence for their ancestors before putting it to use—how could the "Monthly Ordinances" (Yueling) not record this …

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
以示人乎且夫當仲春之月正陽壯之時物皆
產育非若仲冬之閉塞也氣皆宣吐非若季冬
之栗烈也天子於斯時也意謂向者水泉凝冱
既取氷而納之矣今豈可未有所獻而遽開乎
向者水澤腹堅既鑿氷而藏之矣今豈可未有
所祭而遽取乎於是曰殺羔羊以獻於司寒也
而後開既有肥羜以祭於玄冥也而後取然而
氷非徒取將以供夫日用也氷非徒開將以供
夫喪祭也雖所以備用而祖先為尤重故未遑
===
自奉而先薦於寢廟之中雖所以供祭而祖考
為尤尊故未遑他祭而先薦於祖考之前達是
誠於幽冥而與春薦韭夏薦麥者同一心罄是
敬於宗祊而與秋薦稻冬薦黍者同一意王者
順時之禮豈不於斯而可見哉抑論之孝子之
於親飲食必先嘗而後進新物必先薦而後食
非獨氷之不敢先用也記禮君子惓惓於此者
以見微之不可忽而其大之有必謹從可知焉
學者可不考哉

以見微之不可忽而其大之有必謹從可知焉

punctuated: 以示人乎？且夫當仲春之月，正陽壯之時，物皆產育，非若仲冬之閉塞也；氣皆宣吐，非若季冬之栗烈也。天子於斯時也，意謂：「向者水泉凝冱，既取氷而納之矣，今豈可未有所獻而遽開乎？向者水澤腹堅，既鑿氷而藏之矣，今豈可未有所祭而遽取乎？」於是曰殺羔羊以獻於司寒也而後開，既有肥羜以祭於玄冥也而後取。然而氷非徒取，將以供夫日用也；氷非徒開，將以供夫喪祭也。雖所以備用，而祖先為尤重，故未遑自奉，而先薦於寢廟之中；雖所以供祭，而祖考為尤尊，故未遑他祭，而先薦於祖考之前。達是誠於幽冥，而與春薦韭、夏薦麥者同一心；罄是敬於宗祊，而與秋薦稻、冬薦黍者同一意。王者順時之禮，豈不於斯而可見哉！抑論之，孝子之於親，飲食必先嘗而後進，新物必先薦而後食，非獨氷之不敢先用也。記禮君子惓惓於此者，以見微之不可忽，而其大之有必謹，從可知焉。學者可不考哉！
translation_en: …to show to the people? Moreover, in the second month of spring, just when the yang force is growing strong, all things are produced and nurtured, unlike the closure and blockage of midwinter; the vital breaths are all released and exhaled, unlike the biting cold of late winter. At this time, the Son of Heaven thinks to himself: "Previously, when the springs and waters froze hard, we took the ice and stored it away; how can we now abruptly open the ice-house without first making an offering? Previously, when the marshes were frozen solid to their depths, we cut the ice and hid it away; how can we now abruptly take it out without first performing a sacrifice?" Thereupon, as it is said, he slaughters a lamb to offer to the Spirit of Cold (Sihan) and only then opens the ice-house; having prepared a fat five-month-old lamb to sacrifice to Xuanming, only then does he take the ice out. Yet the ice is not merely taken out for its own sake—it is to supply daily needs; the ice-house is not merely opened for its own sake—it is to supply funerals and sacrifices. Although it is meant to prepare for general use, the ancestors are of paramount importance; therefore, before finding leisure to serve himself, he first presents it in the rear hall of the ancestral temple. Although it is meant to supply sacrifices, the deceased ancestors are of supreme honor; therefore, before attending to other sacrifices, he first presents it before his ancestors. Conveying this sincerity to the unseen world, he shares the exact same heart as when presenting leeks in spring and wheat in summer; exhausting this reverence in the ancestral temple area, he shares the exact same intent as when presenting rice in autumn and glutinous millet in winter. Can not the True King's rites of following the seasons be seen right here? Furthermore, if we discuss it further, in a filial son's service to his parents, food and drink must first be tasted before being served, and seasonal delicacies must first be presented in offering before being eaten—it is not only ice that he dares not use first for himself. That the gentleman who recorded the rites was so earnestly attentive to this shows that even small matters must not be neglected, from which one may know how carefully great matters must be attended to. How could scholars fail to examine this!

惟人心之所發得其治，故人心之趨向有其所。夫人情易流，不可不治也。聖王既治人情如治田，則人皆有宿道向方之所，豈不如室之有奧乎？記《禮運》者謂：夫人之有情，曰喜、怒焉，曰哀、樂、愛、惡、欲焉，猶地之有田也；聖王之治人情，亦猶農夫之治田也。彼農夫之治田，必先耕之以耒耜，而後種其所當種；聖王之治人情，則修禮以
translation_en:
"Taking human feelings as the field; therefore people take it as their inner sanctum."
Chen Qing 陳清
Associate Examiner, Historiographer of the Hanlin Academy (Bianxiu) Li comments: [Essays on topics from the "Evolution of Rites" ("Liyun") rarely satisfy one's expectations. Coming suddenly upon this piece, its personal grasp of the subject is intimate and the writing is spirited and expansive. The author must be someone who has applied his mind to fundamental learning; reading it inspires respect.]
Associate Examiner, Academician Reader-in-Waiting (Shidu) Liu comments: [On this topic, some focus exclusively on regulating feelings through ritual and rightness, which inevitably leaves omissions; others discuss ritual, rightness, benevolence, and music all together, resulting in vague and disorganized generalizations. This piece alone weighs its words carefully, implicitly revealing the orderly sequence of the sages' teachings from beginning to end. Its elucidation of the word "inner sanctum" (ao) is especially pertinent—something only one well-seasoned in this [?] Classic could achieve. Therefore it is recorded here as a model for scholars.]
Examiner, Hanlin Academician (Xueshi) Wan comments: [It brings out the meaning of "as the field" and "as the inner sanctum" almost exhaustively, leaving nothing unexpressed.]

text:
耕之而欲七情之中節陳義以種之而使七情
之得宜焉農夫之治田必先耨之以去草而後
聚之以收藏聖王之治人情則講學以耨之而
不使邪僻害其情之正本仁以聚之而必使天
理之公純於心焉人情有所治如此殆見向也
人欲宿道而無其所今焉莫不欲操其禮由於
義而至於仁則宿道有所如室之有奧也昔也

…plows it, desiring that the seven emotions hit their proper measure, and sets forth righteousness to plant it, causing the seven emotions to attain their appropriateness. When a farmer cultivates a field, he must first weed it to remove the grass, and afterward gather the harvest to store it away; when the sage-king cultivates human emotions, he expounds learning to weed them, so as not to let perversity and depravity harm the rectitude of those emotions, and he roots them in benevolence to gather them in, ensuring that the impartiality of Heavenly principle is pure within the mind. When human emotions are cultivated in this way, we see that whereas formerly people wished to abide in the Way yet had no place to do so, now there is no one who does not wish to hold fast to ritual, proceed through righteousness, and arrive at benevolence—thus they have a place to abide in the Way, just as a house has its inner recess (ao). Whereas in the past the common people wished to turn toward the right direction yet had nowhere to do so, now there is no one who does not wish to engage in learning, rely on benevolence, and arrive at joy—thus they have a place toward which to turn, just as a dwelling has its inner recess. When the orientation of the people's minds is like this, there is no emotion that is not rectified, and the sage-king's establishment of laws to bring about governance has also reached the utmost perfection. On the whole, this chapter discusses how when the sage establishes standards, he must root them in the creative transformations of nature and corroborate them with human emotions and the principles of things, each having its verification, and nothing is done carelessly. Therefore, having at the beginning of the chapter spoken of what he takes as his model, what he employs, and what he brings about, upon reaching this point it goes on to speak by analogy of how these are verified. His establishment of laws is complete, his practice of governance is detailed, and the response of auspicious signs may also be said to have reached the utmost. Yet if we seek one who is able to attain this, were he not a sage possessing both virtue and position, how could he be worthy of speaking of it?

無息是之謂強而強又非強此孝乎夫五者備

punctuated:
親者，必為所當為，無一行之或乖，斯可以為義，非義者宜此孝乎？信則不欺，而為子者，必表裏誠實，無一念之或僞，斯可以為信，非信者信此孝乎？自幼至長，力行而不怠；由壯及老，黽勉而無息，是之謂強，而強又非強此孝乎？夫五者備矣，人能體而不變，忘其倦怠之心，是能順從孝道而無違者也。將見日用之間，心廣體胖，仰不愧于天；行己之際，心安理得，俯不怍于人。其喜意之孚，不啻如春陽之布而不能禦；歡欣之發，不啻若草木之茂而莫可遏，此其為樂，可勝言哉！雖然，人徒知德成於孝，而不知教民之本亦不外乎孝；人徒知樂生於孝，而不知刑戮之加亦由背乎孝。故此章之上，既曰「衆之本教曰孝」，下文又曰「刑自反此作」，勸戒之意深矣。厥後孟子推原仁、智、禮、樂之實，亦以事親為言，其有得於此者歟！

第貳場
論
translation_en:
…one's parents must do what ought to be done, without a single action going astray; only thus can it be counted as righteousness. Is this not how righteousness makes this filial piety fitting? Trustworthiness means not deceiving, and one who is a son must be sincere and honest inside and out, without a single thought being false; only thus can it be counted as trustworthiness. Is this not how trustworthiness makes this filial piety true? From childhood to adulthood, practicing it vigorously without slackening; from one's prime to old age, striving diligently without cease—this is called strength, and is strength not strengthening this filial piety? Now when these five are complete, and a person can embody them without changing, forgetting any feeling of weariness or indolence, he is one who is able to follow the way of filial piety without violation. Then in daily life, his mind will be broad and his body at ease, looking up with no shame before Heaven; in conducting himself, his heart will be at peace and principle attained, looking down with no embarrassment before men. The welling up of his joyful spirit is nothing less than the spreading of spring sunshine, which cannot be held back; the burgeoning of his delight is nothing less than the luxuriant growth of plants and trees, which cannot be checked. Could the joy of this ever be fully expressed in words? Even so, people merely know that virtue is brought to completion in filial piety, yet do not know that the foundation of instructing the common people also lies in nothing other than filial piety; people merely know that joy is born of filial piety, yet do not know that the imposition of punishments and executions also stems from turning one's back on filial piety. Therefore, earlier in this passage it is said, "The fundamental teaching for the multitude is called filial piety," and the text below further says, "Punishments arise from going contrary to this." Profound indeed is the intent to encourage and to warn! Thereafter, when Mengzi traced the substance of benevolence, wisdom, propriety, and music, he too spoke of them in terms of serving one's parents—did he not derive his insight from this?

… the equilibrium and harmony of the single mind; and by establishing the equilibrium and harmony of the single mind so as to bring about the equilibrium and harmony of an entire age, one is thereby able to fulfill great and active undertakings without failing the abundant favor and care of High Heaven. In former times, the Han Confucian scholar Ni Kuan 兒寬 spoke of this; I, in my simplicity, beg to elaborate upon his argument.

Now, when pleasure, anger, sorrow, and joy are stored within and have not the slightest leaning to one side, this is the equilibrium of our nature. If equilibrium is not established, then the great foundation cannot stand. When pleasure, anger, sorrow, and joy are expressed outwardly and all hit their proper measure, this is the harmony of our feelings. If harmony is not established, then the universal path cannot be practiced. Therefore, in stillness the sage preserves and nourishes it with reverence, making sure that before feelings are aroused there is not the slightest leaning to one side and that what he holds fast to is not lost; thus in stillness there is not a single breath that is not in equilibrium, and the supreme standard of equilibrium is established. In movement he examines and reflects upon it with reverence, making sure that when responding to things there is not the slightest error or discrepancy and that nowhere is it otherwise; thus in movement there is not a single affair that is not in harmony, and the supreme standard of harmony is established.

From this, he extends this equilibrium to institute rites, so that great rites share the same equilibrium as Heaven and Earth; all the ceremonies of auspicious, inauspicious, military, guest, and joyous occasions, which serve as the instruments for regulating [?] human minds, are none other than the workings of this equilibrium. From this, he extends this harmony to create music, so that great music shares the same harmony as Heaven and Earth; all the notes of gong, shang, jue, zhi, and yu, which serve as the instruments for molding human minds, are none other than the workings of this harmony. Once equilibrium takes form in rites, [there is that whereby]…

以中天下之不中和形於樂矣而有以感
天下之不和自其家而言之則極底豫之
孝致刑于之化而宮庭雍雍然焉舉家皆
中和也自其朝而言之則堂陛森嚴班行
肅睦而百僚師師然焉舉朝皆中和也貴
賤有章長幼有序行者讓路耕者讓畔而
中和充於一國之內矣協和萬邦修和有
夏四海奠枕九宇迓衡而中和溢乎普天
之下矣嘉祥叶氣磅礴於兩間美化淳風
===

於如此何莫非本之天子之一身始乎漢
之武帝雄才大畧固亦美矣然知慕古而
不知所以慕慕其末而不慕其本也故號
令文章雖顯設於朝廷之上而內多私欲
鹵莽多矣典章制度雖輝煌於政治之間
而外假仁義闊畧甚矣是烏足以言極之
建乎寬之舉是以告其所以規之者可謂

以中天下之不中；和形於樂矣，而有以感天下之不和。自其家而言之，則極底豫之孝，致刑于之化，而宮庭雍雍然焉，舉家皆中和也。自其朝而言之，則堂陛森嚴，班行肅睦，而百僚師師然焉，舉朝皆中和也。貴賤有章，長幼有序，行者讓路，耕者讓畔，而中和充於一國之內矣。協和萬邦，修和有夏，四海奠枕，九宇迓衡，而中和溢乎普天之下矣。嘉祥叶氣，磅礴於兩間；美化淳風，滃鬱於八表。建中和之極，其功用之大至於如此，何莫非本之天子之一身始乎？

漢之武帝，雄才大畧，固亦美矣。然知慕古而不知所以慕，慕其末而不慕其本也。故號令文章，雖顯設於朝廷之上，而內多私欲，鹵莽多矣；典章制度，雖輝煌於政治之間，而外假仁義，闊畧甚矣。是烏足以言極之建乎？寬之舉是以告，其所以規之者可謂切，而望之者可謂深矣。惜乎其君不足以
translation_en:
…so as to bring equilibrium to all that lacks equilibrium in the world; and when harmony is given form in music, there is that whereby to move all that lacks harmony in the world. Speaking in terms of his family, he perfects the filial piety that brings parents to delight and achieves the transforming influence of setting a marital example, so that the palace court is filled with concord, and the entire family is in equilibrium and harmony. Speaking in terms of his court, the hall and steps are solemn and majestic, the court ranks are reverent and amicable, and the hundred officials emulate one another, so that the entire court is in equilibrium and harmony. Noble and base have their distinctions, elder and younger have their order, travelers yield the road, and plowmen yield the boundary ridges, so that equilibrium and harmony fill the entire state. He brings harmony to the myriad states and cultivates harmony throughout China; the four seas rest securely on their pillows and the nine regions welcome peaceful governance, so that equilibrium and harmony overflow throughout the whole world under heaven. Auspicious omens and harmonious ether pervade heaven and earth; fine transformations and pure customs flourish abundantly across the eight directions. That the great efficacy of establishing the ultimate standard of equilibrium and harmony reaches such a degree—how could any of it not originate from the person of the Son of Heaven himself?

Emperor Wu of the Han (Han Wudi 漢武帝), with his heroic talent and grand strategy, was indeed admirable. Yet he knew to admire antiquity without knowing how it ought to be admired—admiring its superficial branches rather than its fundamental root. Therefore, although ordinances and literary forms were prominently displayed at court, inwardly he harbored many selfish desires and there was much carelessness; although statutes and institutions shone brilliantly in his governance, outwardly he merely borrowed the semblance of benevolence and righteousness and was exceedingly negligent. How could this suffice to speak of establishing the ultimate standard? In bringing this forward to advise him, Ni Kuan (兒寬) offered counsel that may be called earnest, and expectations that may be called profound. Alas, his sovereign was not worthy of…

…be spoken to of this! That being so, are not the only ones capable of establishing the standard of equilibrium and harmony the Two Emperors and Three Kings of antiquity? Are they not our August Ming's One Founder and Four Ancestors? Reverently considering that the reigning Son of Heaven has gloriously received the precious calendar, and that his governance and transformative influence are splendid and bright: there is no need to draft the rituals of gold-paste and jade-tallies, for his moral virtue naturally surpasses that of a hundred kings; there is no need to compose the songs of the "Fungus Chamber" and the "Precious Tripod," for his achievements are sufficient to be handed down for ten thousand generations. Your servant Zhen Dexiu humbly considers: The Way of the Great Learning (Daxue) has been handed down from thousands of years in the distant past; the supremely sage ruler deeply accords with it within the ninefold precincts of the palace. I venture to expound its meaning so as to exhaust my humble thoughts.

I reverently reflect that Your Majesty [〇〇〇〇] is endowed by Heaven with sagely gifts and daily renews the supreme virtue. In resplendent brilliance and profound wisdom, You match the excellence of Shun of Yu; in gentle grace and admirable reverence, You equal the splendor of King Wen of Zhou. As for the esoteric purport transmitted between Confucius and Zengzi, and the subtle words elucidated by the Cheng brothers and Zhu Xi, You have surely immersed Your profound heart in them, so as to manifest them in transformative governance. Yet the classic of the Sage and the commentary of the Worthy must be verified by recent events before they are easily understood; the virtue of Emperors and the achievements of Kings must conform to this book before they become imperishable.

Your servant has therefore searched widely through earlier canons and compiled this present work, first setting forth the major outlines and then unfolding the numerous subheadings. The rise and fall of states past and present, and what Confucian wise men have censured or praised—arranged like overlapping fish scales and converging wheel-spokes in hundreds and thousands of entries, divided and set out in order across forty-three chapters (juan). It is as when the framework of the Hall of Light (Mingtang) has been fixed and its doors and windows are arrayed side by side; or as when the avenues and thoroughfares of the Sacred Capital have been completed, reaching out on all sides to Chinese and non-Chinese alike. 第一問
章愚
translation_en:
… assist Your sagely intelligence on high. Having chosen an auspicious day, I respectfully present it for the Imperial perusal. In olden times, the Memorial on Peace and Order (Zhi'an shu) was submitted by Jia Yi, yet Emperor Wen of Han did not carry its use through to the end; the Policy Proposals for Great Peace (Taiping ce) were presented by Wang Tong, yet the progenitor of the Sui rejected and did not employ them. Lamenting how rarely those worthy ministers met with appreciation, I rejoice in the fortunate encounter with an enlightened sovereign today. I humbly pray that You will condescend to examine this humble insight of mine, and give Your attention to it in moments of leisure from the myriad affairs of state. It will surely be able to add luster to the sun and moon, extending the radiance of Your illumination to the utmost limits of the Four Seas; and assist the creative forces of Heaven and Earth, continuing the enduring succession of the dynasty for a hundred million years. Your servant is overwhelmed with the utmost earnestness and trepidation as he gazes up at Heaven and looks toward Your Sagely Majesty. I respectfully submit the Extended Meaning of the Great Learning (Daxue yanyi) which I have compiled, accompanying this memorial, for the Imperial hearing.

text:

策手也

對聖臣之尊其君也自古而已然
聖君之垂其訓也於今為愈明然則遵洙泗之

===
大誥中褒善之言藹乎春溫曰淵泉其德
海容其物是也而唐鐸非善之著者乎貶
惡之辭肅乎秋殺曰私勝公微愆深罪重
是也而郭桓非惡之尤者乎諭官生身之
恩是章也與孝順事實同一旨而古之孝
順若唐狄仁傑宋岳武穆非身致公輔而
最賢者乎言民知報獲福是章也與為善
陰隲同一意而古之陰隲若漢鄧禹宋曹
彬非慶流苗裔而最顯者乎至若五倫書

恩是章也與孝順事實同一旨而古之孝
順若唐狄仁傑宋岳武穆非身致公輔而
最賢者乎言民知報獲福是章也與爲善

考試官學士劉批：得事實。

對：聖臣之尊其君也，自古而已然；聖君之垂其訓也，於今為愈明。然則遵洙、泗之教，以讀我祖宗之書，豈不切於躬行、宜於世用也哉！嘗觀《大誥》中，褒善之言藹乎春溫，曰「淵泉其德，海容其物」是也，而唐鐸非善之著者乎？貶惡之辭肅乎秋殺，曰「私勝公微，愆深罪重」是也，而郭桓非惡之尤者乎？「諭官生身之恩」是章也，與《孝順事實》同一旨，而古之孝順若唐狄仁傑、宋岳武穆，非身致公輔而最賢者乎？「言民知報獲福」是章也，與《為善陰隲》同一意，而古之陰隲若漢鄧禹、宋曹彬，非慶流苗裔而最顯者乎？至若《五倫書》
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Compiler Zheng comments: The itemized responses are detailed and thorough, not [confined?] by the prompts of the question; he is a master of policy essays.
Associate Examiner Senior Compiler Xing comments: The policy essay thoroughly accounts for the figures involved; most commendable, most commendable.
Examiner Academician Wan comments: The itemized responses cover ancient and modern historical deeds almost exhaustively; it should be selected for inclusion.
Examiner Academician Liu comments: It grasps the historical facts.

Reply: That sage ministers revere their sovereigns has been so since antiquity; that sage sovereigns hand down their instructions is ever more manifest in the present day. This being so, if one follows the teachings of the Zhu and Si rivers [i.e., Confucius] in order to read the books of our Imperial Ancestors, how could this not be relevant to personal conduct and suited to practical use in the world? I have observed that in the Grand Pronouncements (Da gao), the words praising goodness are as genial as the warmth of spring—such as the saying, "Deep as a spring is his virtue, vast as the sea his tolerance of things"—and was not Tang Duo唐鐸 anoutstanding example of such goodness? The words censuring evil are as stern as the chill of autumn—such as the saying, "Selfishness prevails and public-mindedness dwindles; the offenses are deep and the crimes grave"—and was not Guo Huan 郭桓 an extreme example of such evil? The section "Instructing Officials on the Grace of Those Who Bore Them" shares the same purport as the Biographical Accounts of Filial Piety (Xiaoshun shishi); and among the filial of antiquity, were not men like Di Renjie 狄仁傑 of the Tang and Yue Wumu 岳武穆 [Yue Fei 岳飛] of the Song the worthiest of those who personally rose to become high ministers of state? The section "Speaking of Commoners Who Know Recompense and Obtain Blessings" shares the same meaning as the Secret Merits of Doing Good (Weishan yinzhi); and among those of antiquity who accumulated secret merit, were not men like Deng Yu 鄧禹 of the Han and Cao Bin 曹彬 of the Song the most illustrious of those whose blessings flowed down to their descendants? As for the Book of the Five Relationships (Wulun shu)…

punctuated:
之作，則凡古今之嘉言善行無所不載，而祖宗之文臣武將有所必錄。覩其文而廉潔不汚、剛介有守，若劉敏、凌漢，其佐秋官而副憲臺也宜矣；武而建功立業、策勳揚名，若徐達、沐英，其列鼎彝而垂竹帛也當矣。是以庠序之間，衿佩之士，於隆古之籍既旁搜而遠紹，於昭代之規尤莊誦而服行。雖不敢上擬孔子憲章從周之道，固庶幾乎「為下不倍」之義也。愚也生長於鳶飛魚躍之間，涵泳於鳳儀獸舞之澤，於列聖之四書夙夜留心久矣。但望洋滄海，蠡測難窮；仰高太虛，管窺未徧。故於勸戒之旨，聊舉其綱；然於趨避之心，豈昧其塗哉？惟恕其疎且漏焉。

第二問
陸淵之
考試官郎中何批：此作得周、孔、孟之遺意矣。
translation_en:
… was composed, there were no fine words or good deeds from antiquity to the present that were not included, and the civil officials and military generals of our Imperial Ancestors were unfailingly recorded. When one observes those in the civil service who were incorruptible and untainted, upright and steadfast in their integrity, such as Liu Min 劉敏 and Ling Han 凌漢, it was indeed fitting that they assisted the Ministry of Justice and served as Vice Censors-in-Chief in the Censorate! And as for those in the military who established great achievements and enterprises, registering their merit and spreading their fame, such as Xu Da 徐達 and Mu Ying 沐英, it was truly proper that they were inscribed on sacrificial tripods and vessels and handed down on bamboo and silk! Therefore, within the schools, the scholars wearing collared gowns and girdle pendants not only search broadly into and carry forward from afar the texts of high antiquity, but also reverently recite and faithfully practice the regulations of our illustrious dynasty. Although they dare not compare themselves above to Confucius's way of modeling himself on the Zhou and following the Zhou, they certainly come close to the principle that "being in a lower position, one does not rebel."

Born and raised amidst a world where kites fly and fishes leap, and steeped in thebeneficent age where phoenixes posture and beasts dance, I have for a long time devoted my mind morning and night to these four books of our successive Sacred Emperors. Yet gazing across the vast ocean, it is hard to fathom its depths with a calabash; looking up at the lofty empyrean, one cannot take it all in through a narrow tube. Thus, regarding the purport of their exhortations and warnings, I have merely outlined the main points; yet as for the mind that knows what to pursue and what to avoid, how could I be blind to its path? I ask only that you forgive my cursoriness and omissions.

… admirable is his dedication to the learning of Confucius and Mencius [?].
Associate Examiner Junior Compiler Wu comments: He reconciles one by one the points where the words and deeds of Confucius and Mencius differ; none without a clear grasp of principle could do this.
Associate Examiner Junior Compiler Zhang comments: All five policy essays are concise and vigorous, restraining their sharp edge without ostentation, unlike those in the examination compound who merely indulge in empty rhetoric. This piece is recorded especially for its detailed treatment of the facts.
Examiner Academician Wan comments: He is able to answer point by point regarding the words and deeds of Confucius and Mencius without the slightest hesitation; none who had not devoted his mind to the learning of the sages and worthies could do this.
Examiner Academician Liu comments: Regarding the doubts raised by men of the past about Mencius, Hui'an (Zhu Xi 朱熹) once refuted them one by one; this paper must be by someone who has gained insight from those explanations.

Response: Are the words and deeds of the sages and worthies truly the same? Yet to those who cling to their outward traces, they seem as far apart as spear and shield. Are they truly different? Yet to those who grasp their minds, they match like the halves of a tally. For although the words and deeds of the sages and worthies may seem different, their minds have never been different. If one merely clings to their outward traces without grasping their minds, one will see only their differences and not their sameness—how could that be the way to observe the sages and worthies well! Allow me to set this forth point by point in accordance with your enlightened question. The book of the Mencius (Mengzi) was composed on the model of the Analects (Lunyu), so the words and deeds recorded therein ought to have no differences between them. Yet among them there are very many differences. Let us first discuss them in terms of their deeds: First, in the matter of a ruler's summons—Confucius in Lu received a summons and immediately set out, whereas Mencius in Qi heard the command and did not …

punctuated: 果，一去一不去，何不同歟？盖孔子甞為司冦，魯君召以其官，則不可不亟往；孟子位居賓師，齊王召而託疾，則不可以輕往也。或去或不去，各有道焉。一去國也，孔子於衛，明决於一朝；孟子於齊，濡滯於三宿。一遲一速，何不同歟？盖孔子知靈公决不用己，故意無顧惜；孟子念齊王足與為善，故心復繾綣也。或遲或速，各有宜焉。至於原憲為孔子宰，不容其辭九百之粟，盖有常禄不當辭之義存焉；孟子為齊上卿，不肯受十萬之禄，盖有道不行不當受之意寓焉。此其行雖不同，而心無不同然也。以其言觀之：均之論樂也，孔子取《韶》樂之善美，孟子同俗樂於先王，似相背矣。殊不知孔子之論，乃古今之定制、經世之常言；孟子之論，因齊王之所好、救時之急務也。或取或不取，豈好異歟？均之論大人也，孔子教人畏之，孟子教人藐之，似相戾矣。殊不知
translation_en: …follow through. One went and one did not go—why the difference? It is because Confucius had served as Minister of Justice (sikou 司寇), so when the ruler of Lu summoned him by virtue of his office, he could not fail to go immediately; whereas Mencius occupied the position of an honored guest and teacher, so when the King of Qi summoned him, he pleaded illness because he could not lightly go. Whether going or not going, each had its principle. In the same matter of leaving a state, Confucius in Wei made a clear decision to leave in a single morning, while Mencius in Qi lingered for three nights. One was slow and one was swift—why the difference? It is because Confucius knew that Duke Ling 靈公 would certainly not employ him, and thus had no regrets in his mind; whereas Mencius reflected that the King of Qi was capable of doing good, and thus his heart remained deeply attached. Whether slow or swift, each had what was fitting. As for Yuan Xian 原憲 serving as Confucius's steward, Confucius would not allow him to decline the nine hundred measures of grain, because therein lay the righteous principle that a regular stipend ought not to be declined; whereas when Mencius served as a Senior Minister in Qi, he refused to accept the stipend of one hundred thousand measures, because therein was lodged the intention that when the Way is not put into practice, a stipend ought not to be accepted. Thus, although their actions differed, their minds were no different. Looking at it from their words: Both equally discussed music, yet Confucius approved of the perfection and beauty of the Shao 韶 music, while Mencius equated popular music with the music of the former kings, which seem to contradict one another. Yet people fail to realize that Confucius's discussion represents the fixed standard of past and present and the constant words for ordering the world, whereas Mencius's discussion accommodated what the King of Qi was fond of as an urgent task for rescuing the times. Whether approving or not approving, how could it be out of a fondness for being different? Both equally discussed "great men" (daren 大人), yet Confucius taught people to stand in awe of them, while Mencius taught people to look down upon them, which seem to clash with one another. Yet people fail to realize that…

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
孔子所云大人乃天命之所在者不畏之
則不足以盡修己之誠孟子所云大人乃
爵位之烜赫者不藐之則無以舒展意氣
而盡所言也或畏或不畏豈故乖歟至於
受圍匡人孔子固取必於己矣而未喪斯
文之言亦未嘗不婦諸天孟子見沮臧氏
固取必於天矣而舍我其誰之語亦未嘗
不求諸己此其所言雖不同而心無不同
然也雖然孔孟言行不同又不特明問所
===
及而已他如孔子於南子則亦見孟子則
不肯見諸侯孔子於仁聖則不居孟子則
自言承三聖孔子於昭公知禮之答則直
受為過而不辯孟子於齊宋餽金之問則
力辯其皆是其或見或不見或任或不任
或辯或不辯在聖人宜如此在賢人則不
得不然焉抑烏可一槩泥其跡而疑其心
之不同乎泥其跡而疑其心是不可與論
聖賢者矣敢以是為明問復

之不同乎泥其跡而疑其心是不可與論

punctuated: 孔子所云「大人」，乃天命之所在者，不畏之則不足以盡修己之誠；孟子所云「大人」，乃爵位之烜赫者，不藐之則無以舒展意氣而盡所言也。或畏或不畏，豈故乖歟？至於受圍匡人，孔子固取必於己矣，而「未喪斯文」之言，亦未嘗不婦諸天；孟子見沮臧氏，固取必於天矣，而「舍我其誰」之語，亦未嘗不求諸己。此其所言雖不同，而心無不同然也。雖然，孔孟言行不同，又不特明問所及而已。他如孔子於南子則亦見，孟子則不肯見諸侯；孔子於仁聖則不居，孟子則自言承三聖；孔子於昭公知禮之答，則直受為過而不辯，孟子於齊、宋餽金之問，則力辯其皆是。其或見或不見，或任或不任，或辯或不辯，在聖人宜如此，在賢人則不得不然焉。抑烏可一槩泥其跡而疑其心之不同乎？泥其跡而疑其心，是不可與論聖賢者矣。敢以是為明問復。
translation_en:
…what Confucius calls "great men" are those in whom the Mandate of Heaven resides; if one does not stand in awe of them, one cannot fully realize the sincerity of self-cultivation. What Mencius calls "great men" are those of resplendent rank and position; if one does not look down upon them, one has no way to expand one's spirit and speak one's mind to the fullest. That one stood in awe while the other did not—was this out of willful perversity? As for being surrounded by the men of Kuang, Confucius certainly relied with certainty upon himself, yet in his words about Heaven "not destroying this culture," he also never failed to attribute it to Heaven [婦=歸]. When Mencius was thwarted by the Zang clan, he certainly relied with certainty upon Heaven, yet in his remark, "If not me, then who?", he also never failed to seek it within himself. Thus, although what they said was different, their minds were no different in being so.

Even so, the differences in the words and deeds of Confucius and Mencius are not limited merely to what Your enlightened question has touched upon. In other cases, for example, Confucius even granted an audience to Nanzi, whereas Mencius refused to go see the feudal lords; Confucius declined to claim benevolence and sageliness for himself, whereas Mencius declared that he succeeded the Three Sages; regarding his reply that Duke Zhao knew ritual propriety, Confucius simply accepted it as a fault without arguing, whereas when questioned about accepting gifts of gold in Qi and Song, Mencius vigorously argued that he was right in both instances. Whether granting an interview or not, whether taking the burden upon oneself or not, whether arguing in defense or not—for the Sage it was fitting to act in one way, while for the Worthy he had no choice but to act in the other. How, then, can one sweepingely cling to their outward traces and doubt that their minds were the same? One who clings to their outward traces and doubts their minds is someone with whom one cannot discuss Sages and Worthies. I venture to offer this as my reply to Your enlightened question.

Third Question
Yan Xuan 顏瑄
Comment by Associate Examiner, Bureau Director He 何: What this policy essay answers essentially holds that when a minister is loyal to his ruler, even though he may have other flaws, in the end those cannot obliterate the reality of his loyalty to his ruler. Impartial public opinion truly has its grounding here; therefore, I record this to serve as encouragement for those in the world who render loyal service.
Comment by Associate Examiner, Historiographer Wu 吳: In all five policy essays, his talent and vigor are full and substantial, and the piece discussing loyalty is especially fitting. Only when one possesses such a heart does one utter such words. When he holds office in the future, how could he be willing to fail his ruler?
Comment by Associate Examiner, Historiographer Zhang 張: The policy essay is detailed and comprehensive, and his talent and thought flow abundantly; it is surely not something a fledgling scholar could attain.
Comment by Examiner, Academician Wan 萬: The deeds and realities of loyal ministers of antiquity are set forth point by point without omission; moreover, in his aspirations he befriends only the lofty and enlightened. In the future, when he receives his stipend [or: takes up his duty], he will certainly not be remiss in his affairs; that he will be a devoted minister is clear indeed.
Comment by Examiner, Academician Liu 劉: Even among the ancients worthy of praise, he selects examples to serve as encouragement and warning; his aspiration is grand indeed.
Reply: Discussing the reputation of a loyal minister is not as good as seeking the reality of his deeds; seeking the reality of a loyal minister is not as good as examining his heart. Where there is such a heart, there will be such reality, and reputation will follow it as well. Those in the world who discuss loyal ministers are all blind to this—how could this not have prompted the inquiry sent down by Your Excellency? Now, when the Duke of Zhou 周公 assisted King Cheng 成王, with the supreme virtue of a great sage…

管蔡之毀然德音不瑕赤舄几几其名何
損乎名之爲上忠者宜也非妄也管仲之

雖不能逃於聖人之譏然九合諸侯一匡

非虛也若夫馬援舍隴西之子陽而歸炎

translation_en:
…supreme virtue, and was a close relative of the royal house. Although he could not avoid the slander of the rumors spread by Guan and Cai, his virtuous reputation remained unblemished and he wore his red slippers with composed dignity—how was his good name diminished? To name him among the "Supremely Loyal" (shangzhong) is fitting, and not extravagant. When Guan Zhong (管仲) assisted Duke Huan [of Qi], he received the title of Father Chief Minister [reading 仲父 for 宰父] and bore the responsibility of chief counselor. Although his smallness of capacity could not escape the criticism of the Sage [Confucius], he assembled the feudal lords nine times and brought order to the entire realm—whose achievements were greater than his? To regard him as among the "Secondarily Loyal" (cizhong) is also fitting, and not unfounded.

As for Ma Yuan (馬援), he abandoned Ziyang [Gongsun Shu 公孫述] in Longxi and gave his allegiance to Emperor Guangwu of the fiery Han; in that auspicious meeting of wind and clouds, they clasped hands in mutual delight. Yet why was it that after he had returned from the campaign in Jiaozhi and his achievement of the bronze pillars was already established, just as his carts were loaded with job's-tears, slander about pearls and rhinoceros horn suddenly arose? Those who slandered him merely disgraced themselves—what fault was it of Yuan's? If he were not given the posthumous title "Loyal and Accomplished" (Zhongcheng), then who should be? Zhuge Liang (諸葛亮), known as the Sleeping Dragon, was moved by the earnestness of [Liu Bei's] three visits; the encounter of ruler and minister was as harmonious as fish and water. Yet why was it that just after his Memorials on Dispatching the Troops had been submitted, a star fell at the camp gate; and just after he had sent the gift of a woman's headdress [to taunt Sima Yi], the gibe that he ate little and handled too many affairs came true? Those who mocked him merely mocked themselves—what detriment was it to Liang? If he were not given the posthumous title "Loyal and Martial" (Zhongwu), then who should be?

As for Xu Yougong (徐有功), although in person he served the Zhou [of Empress Wu], his intent was to preserve the Tang; he cannot be called one who merely curried favor to get by. Pei, Duke of Jin [Pei Du 裴度], had the safety and peril of the state bound up in his own person, while his ambition remained fixed on restoration; how…

可謂之無謀乎？一則褒以「忠正」，一則「文忠」，孰謂不當焉？又如寇萊公之扈從澶淵，羽書交至而飲笑自如，人皆以為燕；然能却戎狄、保社稷，何病乎？韓魏公之執政三朝，而險阻不避，人皆以為專；然能定大業、安中外，何專乎？一則號為「大忠」，一則號為「忠勇」，又孰謂不當焉？之數君子，德非不大也，功非不盛也，其才其學非不足以周於身而用於世也。但其心有誠偽，其學有王霸，擇其光明者而師之，狡偽者而戒之，此愚生之素志。執事其進教之，幸甚。

第四問
章懋
同考試官編修鄭〔批：策弊政，欲觀士子學識。此篇論議區畫，皆鑿鑿可行者；末復責之監司，尤為究本之論。識時務者為俊傑，吾於子望之矣。〕
同考試官修撰邢〔批：試本領，既醇既美；陳時□，不激不隨。必知古而知今，真有才而有識。擢魁多士，用〕
translation_en:
…can he be called lacking in counsel? One was praised with the posthumous title "Loyal and Upright" (Zhongzheng), and the other [with] "Cultured and Loyal" (Wenzhong)—who would say these were unfitting? Or take again Duke Lai of Kou (Kou Zhun 寇準), who attended the emperor on the campaign to Chanyuan: feathered dispatches arrived from all sides, yet he drank and laughed with composure. Everyone took this for laxity [? 燕]; yet he was able to repulse the barbarians and preserve the altars of soil and grain—what fault was there in that? Or Duke Wei of Han (Han Qi 韓琦), who held the reins of government through three reigns without shrinking from danger and difficulty. Everyone took this for arbitrariness; yet he was able to settle the great enterprise of the succession and bring peace within and without the court—what arbitrariness was there in that? One was styled "Greatly Loyal" (Dazhong), and the other was styled "Loyal and Valiant" (Zhongyong)—who again would say these were unfitting?

As for these several gentlemen, it is not that their virtue was not great, nor that their achievements were not flourishing, nor that their talent and learning were insufficient to provide for their own persons and be of use to the world. However, in their minds there was sincerity or falsity, and in their learning there was the Way of the True King or the Way of the Hegemon. To choose those who were illustrious and take them as teachers, and to take those who were crafty and false as a warning—this has been the long-held aspiration of this foolish student. How fortunate it would be should Your Excellency advance and instruct me!

Zhang Mao 章懋

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
協輿情
考試官學士萬批時務一策歴指攸司晚弊之害
而條陳宜行之計誠才識士也况初塲二塲俱優巖之以俟
廷對莫或議矣
考試官學士劉批篇中英英乎有用世之志叅前
後諸篇宜在首選語云賢才出國將昌吾豈特為斯
士喜也哉為我
國家喜而不寐矣
對天下之事在上者能行之在下者能言
之上有資於下之言故不恥於自屈此執
事之心也下有望於上之行故不慙於自
獻此愚生之心也上下交而以成天下之
事者非他也共以圖報于
君父也欽惟
皇上繼體守成厲精圖治慮人材之未興也於
臨御之初親移
玉輅榮賁黌宫其造士之恩渥矣章縫之士
拭目

試目
punctuated:
協輿情。
考試官學士萬批：時務一策，歴指攸司晚弊之害，而條陳宜行之計，誠才識士也。况初塲、二塲俱優，巖之以俟廷對，莫或議矣。
考試官學士劉批：篇中英英乎有用世之志，叅前後諸篇，宜在首選。語云：「賢才出，國將昌。」吾豈特為斯士喜也哉？為我國家喜而不寐矣！
對：天下之事，在上者能行之，在下者能言之。上有資於下之言，故不恥於自屈，此執事之心也；下有望於上之行，故不慙於自獻，此愚生之心也。上下交而以成天下之事者，非他也，共以圖報于君父也。欽惟皇上繼體守成，厲精圖治，慮人材之未興也，於臨御之初，親移玉輅，榮賁黌宫，其造士之恩渥矣！章縫之士，拭目
translation_en:
… so as to accord with public sentiment.

Examiner and Academician Wan 萬 [Wan An 萬安] comments: In this policy essay on current affairs, he successively points out the harms of the recent abuses [?] of the responsible authorities and sets forth point by point the plans that ought to be carried out. Truly, he is a scholar of talent and insight! Moreover, his work in both the first and second sessions was superior. To place him at the top [?] to await the Palace Examination is a decision none could dispute.

Examiner and Academician Liu 劉 [Liu Dingzhi 劉定之] comments: Throughout this piece shines a brilliant aspiration to be of service to the world. Considered alongside his preceding and following papers, he ought to be placed at the head of those selected. As the saying goes, "When worthy talents emerge, the state will prosper." How could I rejoice merely for this scholar alone? For the sake of our dynastic state, I am so overjoyed that I cannot sleep!

Reply: As for the affairs of the realm, those above are able to put them into practice, while those below are able to speak of them. Those above draw upon the words of those below and therefore are not ashamed to humble themselves—such is the mind of Your Excellency. Those below place their hopes in the actions of those above and therefore are not embarrassed to offer their views—such is the mind of this foolish student. That above and below join together in order to accomplish the affairs of the realm is for no other reason than to strive together to repay our Sovereign and Father.

Reverently I reflect that His Majesty, having succeeded to the throne and preserved the achievements of his predecessors, stimulates his spirit to plan for good governance. Concerned that men of talent have not yet risen to prominence, at the very beginning of his reign he personally moved his jade carriage to honor the Imperial College with a visit. Abundant indeed is his grace in cultivating scholars! Scholars in ceremonial dress and broad-stitched robes wipe their eyes to gaze upon …

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
翠華側耳
鸞和荷棫樸之作成樂菁莪之教育莫不勤
于學問宜乎其有成材矣奈何庠序猶縄
而限年四十以拔之几以司教化之未得
其人而然耳誠得其人則經義治事皆有
用之學欂梁榱桷皆適用之材而振淹拔
滯之時宜尚何足以待士也然又患乎農
事之不勤也於東作之時
親祀先農耕籍千畆其勸農之意至矣犂鋤
===
===
之輩覩
朱紘之秉耒樂
冕弁之終畆婦子饁田老稚鋤隴莫不力于
稼穡宜乎其屢豐年矣奈何飢饉相仍而
至遣使再出以賑之凡以司民社者之未
得其人而然耳誠得其人則三年耕必有
一年之食九年耕必有三年之食而散利
薄征之荒政何待於施行乎今之人材皆
出於學校惟其教士之未至是以居官者

薄征之荒政何待於施行乎今之人材皆

punctuated: 翠華，側耳鸞和，荷棫樸之作成，樂菁莪之教育，莫不勤于學問，宜乎其有成材矣。奈何庠序猶縄，而限年四十以拔之？几以司教化之未得其人而然耳。誠得其人，則經義、治事皆有用之學，欂梁、榱桷皆適用之材，而振淹拔滯之時宜，尚何足以待士也？然又患乎農事之不勤也，於東作之時，親祀先農，耕籍千畆，其勸農之意至矣。犂鋤之輩，覩朱紘之秉耒，樂冕弁之終畆，婦子饁田，老稚鋤隴，莫不力于稼穡，宜乎其屢豐年矣。奈何飢饉相仍，而至遣使再出以賑之？凡以司民社者之未得其人而然耳。誠得其人，則三年耕必有一年之食，九年耕必有三年之食，而散利薄征之荒政，何待於施行乎？今之人材，皆出於學校，惟其教士之未至，是以居官者
translation_en:
… at the kingfisher banners and pricking up their ears at the harmonious carriage bells, receiving the nurturing documented in the ode "Bushy Oak-Trees" (Yupu) and rejoicing in the instruction celebrated in the ode "Luxuriant Tarragon" (Jing'e), have without exception applied themselves diligently to learning; by rights, accomplished talents ought to have emerged. Why, then, are those in the local schools still bound [by stagnation] [?], so that an age requirement of forty has been set to select and promote them? All of this is simply because we have not yet found the right men to take charge of moral transformation and education. If we truly obtain the right men, then both classical exegesis and administrative affairs will become practical learning, and both brackets and beams, rafters and eaves-tiles will become useful timber—how then would temporary expedients for rescuing the long-submerged and promoting the stagnating even be needed to treat our scholars?

Yet His Majesty also worried that agriculture was not being pursued with diligence. At the time of spring plowing, he personally sacrificed to the First Agriculturist and plowed the sacred thousand-mu field; his intention to encourage farming could not have been more complete. The common folk with their plows and hoes, beholding the Sovereign in his vermilion cap-cord grasping the plow-handle, and rejoicing as the ceremonial caps and robes completed the furrows—wives and children bringing meals to the fields, the old and young hoeing the ridges—have without exception exerted their strength in sowing and reaping; by rights, there ought to have been repeated years of abundance. Why, then, have famines followed one upon another, to the point that envoys had to be dispatched a second time to provide relief? All of this is simply because we have not yet found the right men to take charge of the people and their altars of the soil. If we truly obtain the right men, then three years of plowing will surely yield one year's surplus of food, and nine years of plowing will surely yield three years' surplus of food—what need would there be to implement famine-relief policies of distributing provisions and lightening imposts?

Today's men of talent all come out of the schools. Only because the instruction of scholars has not yet reached perfection do those who hold office …

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
不修其職而恣肆於郡縣三載之
覲雖曰汰去之多然廉能不一二而貪暴累
千百安能盡汰之乎為今之計莫若慎擇
師儒使之嚴訓迪於未用之時而又精選
舉於將用之際勤考課於既用之後厲廉
恥之節抑奔競之風則吏莫不為循良之
帰而前召父後杜母相望於郡縣矣今之
民命皆懸於守令惟其愛民之乖方是以
為民者不奠其居而弄兵於潢池數年之
===
間雖曰殲殄之眾然蒼鷹之擊搏屠伯之
殘虐幾何不愈望望然而去乎為今之計
莫若慎擇守令使之如龔遂之化渤海黃
霸之治潁川張綱之化廣陵躬撫字之勞
輕繭絲之稅則民莫不懷革面之誠而賣
刀劔買牛犢相安於田里矣雖然民豈樂
於盜哉飢寒切身不得不至於此耳愚甞
思之凡今日之所以召水旱之災致民心
之離者皆不才之守令為之也而守令之

punctuated:
不修其職，而恣肆於郡縣。三載之覲，雖曰汰去之多，然廉能不一二，而貪暴累千百，安能盡汰之乎？為今之計，莫若慎擇師儒，使之嚴訓迪於未用之時，而又精選舉於將用之際，勤考課於既用之後，厲廉恥之節，抑奔競之風，則吏莫不為循良之帰，而前召父、後杜母相望於郡縣矣。

今之民命皆懸於守令，惟其愛民之乖方，是以為民者不奠其居，而弄兵於潢池。數年之間，雖曰殲殄之眾，然蒼鷹之擊搏、屠伯之殘虐，幾何不愈望望然而去乎？為今之計，莫若慎擇守令，使之如龔遂之化渤海、黃霸之治潁川、張綱之化廣陵，躬撫字之勞，輕繭絲之稅，則民莫不懷革面之誠，而賣刀劔、買牛犢，相安於田里矣。

雖然，民豈樂於盜哉？飢寒切身，不得不至於此耳。愚甞思之，凡今日之所以召水旱之災、致民心之離者，皆不才之守令為之也；而守令之
translation_en:
…fail to attend to their duties and act with unbridled license in the prefectures and counties. At the triennial court audiences, although it is said that many are weeded out, the incorrupt and capable are scarcely one or two, while the greedy and tyrannical number in the hundreds and thousands—how could they all be weeded out? The best plan for today is to carefully select Confucian teachers and have them strictly instruct and guide scholars before they are employed; then, to refine the selection process when they are about to be employed, and to diligently conduct performance evaluations after they have been employed. If we encourage a sense of integrity and shame and curb the trend of scrambling for advancement, then officials will all turn into model administrators, and successors to "Father Shao" (Shao Xinchen 召信臣) and "Mother Du" (Du Shi 杜詩) will be seen one after another in the prefectures and counties.

Today, the lives of the people all depend on the prefects and magistrates. Because they go awry in their methods of caring for the people, the common folk cannot settle in their homes and instead take up arms in the marshes. Over the course of several years, although large numbers of them have been annihilated, when faced with the fierce striking of "goshawks" and the cruel tyranny of "butcher lords," how many of the people will not flee ever further away in disappointment? The best plan for today is to carefully select prefects and magistrates, making them like Gong Sui 龔遂 transforming Bohai 渤海, Huang Ba 黃霸 governing Yingchuan 潁川, and Zhang Gang 張綱 transforming Guangling 廣陵—personally taking on the toil of nurturing the people and lightening the "silk-cocoon" tax extractions. Then the people will all harbor a sincere desire to reform themselves, selling their swords and knives to buy oxen and calves, and living together in peace in their fields and villages.

Even so, do the people actually take pleasure in being bandits? With hunger and cold pressing upon their bodies, they simply have no choice but to come to this. I have reflected on this: everything today that brings on disasters of flood and drought and causes the alienation of the people's hearts is the doing of incompetent prefects and magistrates; and the reason prefects and magistrates…

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
所以敢為貪暴者皆不才之監司縱之也
誠使學校之所養皆得其人而又時舉勸
懲之典必不得已如古之賢王烹阿而封
即墨焉自然吏稱其職而民安其業矣尚
何飢寒盜賊之足憂乎管見如斯惟執事
其進教之
第五問
羅倫
同考試官檢討耿批禦戎一策塲中多為所
窘惟此卷條答無遺文勢舂容識見超越所
謂安行於他人窘歩之餘非老於問學者未易語
此一薦何忝
同考試官編修尹批五策敷答詳明詞氣慷
慨此篇尤核而斷所謂有學有識之士進對
大廷未必非裒然出色者
同考試官修撰王批初塲得之已知為有學之士
及觀論策筆力雄健意思沛然深喜不失於驪
黃之外矣禦戎一策尤有發越斷制異時授之以政

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
功業必有可觀者得士如此主司能不為之慶幸
考試官學士萬批禦戎擇將之術滔滔寫出真
博洽有識士乎
考試官學士劉批此卷五策近五千言事核而
辭豐氣充而理直可謂竒士此篇末以韓范自期非
易其言也不言則慮人之不足以知巳也今既知而進之
矣其終守此志勿有怠焉
對備邊者莫要於擇將為將者莫要於知

===
為將而不知兵則士卒何以用其力哉抑
甞觀之中國之有夷狄如陽之有陰不能
無也在防之得其人而已漢之邊患匈奴
為甚於是命衛青霍去病二公出兵以討

公出守以却之韓范本儒生也然韓則寒
西賊之心膽范則有胸中之甲兵此其所

translation_en:
…his achievements in office will surely be well worth beholding. Having obtained a scholar such as this, how could the examiners not rejoice on his account?

Comment by Examiner Academician Wan: The methods for defending against the western barbarians and selecting generals are poured forth in an unstoppable flow—truly a broadly learned and discerning scholar!

Comment by Examiner Academician Liu: The five policy essays in this paper come to nearly five thousand words. The facts are verified and the diction abundant; the vigor is full and the reasoning sound—he may truly be called an extraordinary scholar. At the end of this piece, he models his aspirations on Han Qi (韓琦) and Fan Zhongyan (范仲淹). He does not utter these words lightly; rather, he feared that if he did not speak out, others would not sufficiently recognize his worth. Now that he has been recognized and advanced, may he hold fast to this ambition to the very end and never grow lax.

Reply: For those who prepare the frontier defenses, nothing is more essential than selecting generals; for those who act as generals, nothing is more essential than understanding warfare. Indeed, if one prepares the frontier defenses without selecting the right generals, the enemy will be able to exploit the vulnerabilities; if one acts as a general without understanding warfare, how can the rank-and-file soldiers exert their strength to good effect? Moreover, I have observed that China's having the barbarians is like yang having yin: it is impossible for them not to exist, and everything depends solely on obtaining the right men to guard against them. Among the frontier troubles of the Han dynasty, the Xiongnu were the worst; thereupon the two lords Wei Qing (衛青) and Huo Qubing (霍去病) were ordered to lead troops forth to chastise them. Wei and Huo were originally of menial and servile background; yet Wei honored the worthy and humbled himself before scholars, while Huo devoted himself to the state and forgot his own household, and this was how they struck the Chanyu and won repeated victories. Among the frontier troubles of the Song dynasty, the Western Xia (Xi Xia) was the most pressing; thereupon the two lords Han Qi and Fan Zhongyan were ordered to go out and hold the frontier to repel them. Han and Fan were originally Confucian scholars; yet Han struck chill into the hearts and gall of the western rebels, while Fan possessed tens of thousands of armored soldiers within his own breast, and this was how…

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
以窘曩霄而来臣焉察威猘勒于漠外亦
非廢事也謀定而能暇爾刺客取帶于臥
内韓非弛備也誠著而能感爾此其所由
以成功焉責李廣至自畫者衛所以行将
令非專擅也與元昊通簡書者范所以宣
主德非輕率也亦其所由以成功焉今也
擁鉞以備禦于北者有擾攘之憂握機以
經理于西者有掠虜之虞然則計當焉出
邪彼北虜雖驕也使備禦之者皆衛霍其
===
人則犬羊之虜驕氣自沮而遠遁之不逞
何必與之和而不免細柳之視師也昔漢
之婁敬以和為謀乃和其所不當和和之
者適所以驕之尓彼西羌雖黠也使經理
之者皆韓范其人則蛇豕之羌黠心自銷

之見刦也昔唐之馬燧以盟為請者盟其
所不當盟盟之者適所以黠之尓抑備邊
固在于得将而為將尤在于知兵三代以

以窘曩霄而来臣焉。察威猘勒于漠外，亦非廢事也，謀定而能暇爾；刺客取帶于臥内，韓非弛備也，誠著而能感爾：此其所由以成功焉。責李廣至自畫者，衛所以行将令，非專擅也；與元昊通簡書者，范所以宣主德，非輕率也：亦其所由以成功焉。

今也擁鉞以備禦于北者，有擾攘之憂；握機以經理于西者，有掠虜之虞。然則計當焉出邪？彼北虜雖驕也，使備禦之者皆衛、霍其人，則犬羊之虜驕氣自沮，而遠遁之不逞，何必與之和，而不免細柳之視師也？昔漢之婁敬以和為謀，乃和其所不當和；和之者，適所以驕之尓。彼西羌雖黠也，使經理之者皆韓、范其人，則蛇豕之羌黠心自銷，而請降之不暇，何必與之盟，而恐遭清水之見刦也？昔唐之馬燧以盟為請者，盟其所不當盟；盟之者，適所以黠之尓。

…by which they drove Nangxiao [Yuanhao] into困 distress and brought him to submit as a vassal. Kickball (cuju) being played [?] beyond the desert—this too was not a neglect of duty [by Huo Qubing], but rather that his plans were settled and he could afford to be at leisure; an assassin taking a belt from within the bedchamber—this was not Han Qi relaxing his defenses, but rather that his sincerity was manifest and able to move the man: this was the means by which they achieved success. Holding Li Guang to account to the point that he took his own life [?] was how Wei Qing enforced the commander's orders, not an act of arbitrary authority; exchanging letters with Yuanhao was how Fan Zhongyan proclaimed his sovereign's virtue, not an act of rashness: this too was the means by which they achieved success.

Now, those who hold the battle-axe of command to stand on defense in the north face the worry of disturbances and incursions; those who grasp the levers of strategy to manage affairs in the west face the danger of pillaging and captive-taking. If so, whence should our plan of action come? Although those northern caitiffs are arrogant, if those who defend against them are all men like Wei Qing and Huo Qubing, then the arrogant spirit of the dog-and-sheep caitiffs will naturally be broken and they will flee far away without having time [?], so why must we make peace with them, only to end up unable to avoid inspecting the troops at Xiliu? In the past, Lou Jing of the Han made peace his counsel, yet that was making peace where peace ought not to have been made; making peace with them was precisely what made them arrogant. Although those western Qiang are cunning, if those who manage them are all men like Han Qi and Fan Zhongyan, then the cunning hearts of the snake-and-swine Qiang will naturally melt away and they will have no leisure for anything but begging to surrender, so why must we swear a covenant with them, only to fear suffering the ambush and seizure at Qingshui? In the past, Ma Sui of the Tang requested a covenant, yet that was swearing a covenant where no covenant ought to have been sworn; swearing a covenant with them was precisely what made them cunning.

title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
上兵法之家善者莫若軒轅之五陣三代
以下兵法之家善者莫若孔明之八陣軒
轅五陣本於五行言陣之形勢直陣屬木
銳陣屬火方陣屬土圓陣屬金曲陣屬水
如敵陣為金形我則為火形之陣以克之
敵陣為火形我則為水形之陣以克之此
軒轅之所以為善也孔明八陣本於八卦
言陣之方位天地風雲四陣即乾坤巽艮
四隅卦之寓名也龍虎鳥蛇四陣即震兌
===
離坎四方卦之寓名也正兵出何方則兩
隅竒兵張翼以夾之正兵出何隅則兩方
竒兵掎角以應之擊首則尾應擊尾則首
應擊中則旁至擊旁則中起此孔明之所
以為善也今日擁鉞之貴胄果能此今日
握機之將種果知此乎則胡將無所肆其
驕而何必和羌將無所肆其黠而何必盟
有文事者必有武備是法也武者固不可
以不知而文者亦不可以不講然則衛霍

translation_en:
… and earlier, among masters of the art of war, none excelled the Five Formations of Xuanyuan [the Yellow Emperor]; from the Three Dynasties onward, among masters of the art of war, none excelled the Eight Formations of Kongming [Zhuge Liang 諸葛亮].

Xuanyuan's Five Formations are rooted in the Five Phases and speak of the configurations of formations: the straight formation corresponds to Wood, the pointed formation to Fire, the square formation to Earth, the circular formation to Metal, and the curved formation to Water. For instance, if the enemy's formation is shaped like Metal, we deploy a Fire-shaped formation to overcome it; if the enemy's formation is shaped like Fire, we deploy a Water-shaped formation to overcome it. This is why Xuanyuan's method excels.

Kongming's Eight Formations are rooted in the Eight Trigrams and speak of the directional positions of formations: the four formations of Heaven, Earth, Wind, and Cloud are the figurative names for the trigrams of the four corners—Qian, Kun, Xun, and Gen; the four formations of Dragon, Tiger, Bird, and Snake are the figurative names for the trigrams of the four cardinal directions—Zhen, Dui, Li, and Kan. Whichever cardinal direction the regular troops advance from, the unorthodox troops at the two adjacent corners spread out like wings to flank the enemy; whichever corner the regular troops advance from, the unorthodox troops at the two adjacent cardinal directions form a pincer to support them. Strike the head and the tail responds; strike the tail and the head responds; strike the center and the flanks arrive; strike the flanks and the center rises up. This is why Kongming's method excels.

If today's noble scions who wield the battle-axe can truly practice this, and if today's hereditary generals who hold the mechanisms of command truly understand this, then the northern Hu will have nowhere to indulge their arrogance—so why must we make peace with them? And the Qiang will have nowhere to indulge their cunning—so why must we swear alliances with them? "One who has civil affairs must also have military preparations." As for these methods, military men certainly must not fail to know them, and civil officials likewise must not fail to study them. If that is so, then as for the achievements of Wei [Wei Qing 衛青] and Huo [Huo Qubing 霍去病]…

Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

The second year after His Majesty succeeded to the great imperial heritage was indeed the bingxu year of the Chenghua reign (1466). Now in the second month of spring, it was the scheduled time for the Ministry of Rites to conduct the Metropolitan Examination for tribute scholars from throughout the realm. When the day arrived, Your Servant Kui [Yao Kui 姚夔], the Minister, memorialized to inform the Throne and moreover requested the appointment of Examiners. His Majesty commanded that it be carried out according to precedent, and further decreed that Your Servant Dingzhi [Liu Dingzhi 劉定之] go to take charge of this examination, with Your Servant An [Ke Qian 柯潛, courtesy name Meng'an 孟安, or萬安 Wan An] participating alongside him. Having unworthily received this grand commission, Your Servants were filled with trepidation and allowed ourselves no leisure; together with all the managing officials, we admonished and counselled one another, striving to uphold impartiality in order to gather in the worthy and talented of the realm, hoping to answer His Majesty's generous intention in entrusting us with this charge. title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
鏖戰者三千有竒其能爭鋒
得在選列者三百五十人視
前科盖加多也於戲亦盛矣
哉事既竣例有録
進呈且傳示天下而安宜言于
後仰惟我
國家取士非一途獨科目專以
===

天下大經大法所寓也其間
紀載當時所託臣工不有股

在經惟士通經舉而用焉必
能不曠所託以佐成化理譬

translation_en:
…fought fiercely in the competition numbered more than three thousand; those who proved able to contend at the forefront and attain a place on the list of the selected were three hundred and fifty men, a number even greater than in previous examinations. Alas, how splendid indeed! Now that the affair has been concluded, by precedent a record is to be presented to the throne and circulated throughout the realm, and it is fitting that I, [Liu] An, should append a postface at the end.

Looking up in reflection, our Dynasty does not recruit scholars by a single path alone, yet the civil service examination system selects them exclusively on the basis of scholarship in the Classics. This is truly because the Classics are the repository of the great principles and fundamental laws by which the emperors and kings of antiquity governed the world. Among the officials and ministers recorded therein to whom governance was entrusted in those times, were there not those who served as limbs and arms to the ruler? Those who had charge of acting as his ears and eyes? Those who bore the duty of serving as bulwarks and protective screens? Although those men have passed away, their traces remain in the Classics. translation_en: …like a farmer growing grain or a gardener growing vegetables—how could one fail to effortlessly reap clear results? Thus it is for this reason that the state selects scholars through mastery of the Classics, and for this reason too that scholars must advance to office through elucidating the Classics. People constantly say that scholars are valued by the world simply because they are able to master the Classics and put them to practical use. Therefore, in their engagement with the Classics—probing their depths and reaching a comprehension that merges with their own nature [?]—they cannot depart from them even for a single morning. title: 成化二年會試錄
text:
選明將悉本之經以對敭
臨軒之問而股肱而耳目而藩
垣屏翰之託靡或不得也而
可獨違乎經邪尚隨所任使
極力體行之上以輔翊化原
下以膏澤黎庶俾楙績芳聲
洸洸乎赫赫乎能追躅往古
===
所託臣工於千百載上將千
百載而下人孰不曰
國家以經術取士果得真才之
用士之通經果足以周世之
用夫然於科目不有光與不
有光與謹書此與諸士相底
厲云

厲云
punctuated: 選。明將悉本之經，以對敭臨軒之問，而股肱、而耳目、而藩垣屏翰之託，靡或不得也，而可獨違乎經邪？尚隨所任使，極力體行之，上以輔翊化原，下以膏澤黎庶，俾楙績芳聲，洸洸乎、赫赫乎，能追躅往古所託臣工於千百載上。將千百載而下，人孰不曰：「國家以經術取士，果得真才之用；士之通經，果足以周世之用。」夫然，於科目不有光與？不有光與？謹書此與諸士相底厲云。
translation_en:
…selected. Soon, you will draw entirely upon the Classics to respond to and extol the Emperor's inquiries at the Palace Examination, and there is no charge—whether as his limbs and torso, his ears and eyes, or his protective bulwarks and screens—that you might not receive. How, then, could you possibly depart from the Classics?

May you, in whatever office you are assigned, exert your utmost to embody and practice them: above, to assist the source of moral transformation, and below, to shower beneficence upon the common people, so that yoursplendid achievements and fragrant reputations, grand and illustrious, may rival in the footsteps of those ministers and officials entrusted in antiquity hundreds and thousands of years ago. Then, hundreds and thousands of years from now, who will not say: "In selecting scholars through classicist learning, the dynasty truly obtained the service of genuine talent; and the scholars' mastery of the Classics was truly sufficient to meet the needs of the age"? If it is thus, will this not bring glory to the examination system? Will it not bring glory indeed? I respectfully write this to encourage and sharpen you scholars.
